tummy_time.name: Tummy time
tummy_time.goal: Holds their head up during tummy time.
tummy_time.why: Time on the tummy while awake builds the neck, shoulder and back strength needed for rolling, sitting and crawling.
steps: Pick a moment when your baby is awake and content, not straight after a feed.
Lay your baby on their tummy on a blanket on the floor, or on your chest.
Get down to their eye level. Talk, smile or hold a bright toy in front of their face.
Start with 1 or 2 minutes, 2 or 3 times a day, and build up to about 15 to 30 minutes a day in total. Stay with your baby the whole time.
Turn your baby onto their back when they get tired or fussy.
avoid: Tummy time when your baby is sleepy. Always put your baby to sleep on their back.
Leaving your baby alone on their tummy, even for a moment.
Soft surfaces such as pillows or a sofa.
tummy_time.success: Your baby lifts their head for a moment, even if it wobbles.
ways: On your chest while you lie back and talk.
On a blanket with a baby-safe mirror in front.
Across your lap while you gently pat their back.

follow_toy.name: Follow the toy
follow_toy.goal: Watches you or a toy as it moves.
follow_toy.why: Following a moving object trains the eyes, attention and the first steps of coordination.
steps: Lay your baby on their back on a safe, flat surface.
Hold a bright toy or rattle about 30 cm from their face. Wait until your baby looks at it.
Move it slowly to one side, then back to the middle.
Do the same to the other side, then up and down.
Smile and praise your baby when their eyes follow.
avoid: Moving the toy too fast for the eyes to keep up.
Holding it very close to their face.
Continuing when your baby looks away. It means they need a break.
follow_toy.success: Your baby looks at the toy for a few seconds and follows it a little to one side.
ways: Your own face, moving slowly side to side.
A rattle shaken gently off to one side, so your baby turns to the sound.
A colourful cloth book moved up and down.

talk_back.name: Talk back and forth
talk_back.goal: Makes sounds back when you talk.
talk_back.why: Copying your baby's sounds and waiting for an answer is the first conversation. It builds the base for speech.
steps: Hold your baby face to face, close enough for them to see your mouth.
Wait for a sound such as "ooo" or "aah".
Copy the sound back, with a smile.
Pause. Give your baby time to answer.
Keep the turns going for a few rounds, then rest.
avoid: Talking without pauses, so there is no turn for your baby.
Background noise from a TV or radio.
Continuing when your baby turns away.
talk_back.success: Your baby watches your face and makes a sound after you stop.
ways: During nappy changes.
During a bath, copying splashes and sounds.
Singing a short song and pausing before the last word.

reach_grab.name: Reach and grab
reach_grab.goal: Reaches for a toy they want.
reach_grab.why: Reaching and grabbing connects the eyes and hands, and teaches your baby that they can make things happen.
steps: Sit your baby with support, or lay them on their back on a blanket.
Hold a soft, easy-to-grip toy within your baby's reach.
Wait and let your baby swing or reach for it.
Let your baby touch and hold it. Give it to them if they get close.
Praise and repeat with the toy on the other side.
avoid: Toys small enough to swallow, or with sharp parts.
Holding the toy too far away, which makes the game frustrating.
Pulling the toy away as a tease.
reach_grab.success: Your baby swings an arm towards the toy or touches it.
ways: A rattle placed in their hand, then held just out of reach.
Hanging toys on a play gym.
A soft ball rolled slowly towards their hands.

roll_over.name: Roll over
roll_over.why: Rolling is the first way your baby moves on their own. It builds strength for sitting and crawling.
steps: Lay your baby on their tummy on a blanket on the floor.
Hold a favourite toy just out of reach, to one side and slightly up.
Move the toy slowly across so your baby turns to follow it.
Help a little by guiding their hip if your baby gets stuck halfway.
Cheer when your baby rolls, then try the other side.
avoid: Practising on a bed or changing table. Rolling babies can fall.
Pushing your baby all the way over.
Long sessions. A few tries are enough.
roll_over.success: Your baby turns their head and shoulders towards the toy.
ways: A toy that makes a sound when it moves.
Your face to one side, calling your baby's name.
A baby-safe mirror placed to one side.

pull_stand.name: Pull up to stand
pull_stand.why: Standing comes before cruising along furniture and walking. It builds leg and trunk strength.
steps: Choose a soft, safe spot beside a sturdy sofa or low table. Check that it cannot tip.
Sit your baby on the floor in front of it. Put a favourite toy on top.
Make sure your baby can see the toy. Do not lift your baby.
Wait. Say "Up you come." Offer a hand only if your baby reaches for it.
Praise your baby for standing, even for 3 seconds. Help your baby sit back down gently.
avoid: Pulling your baby up by the arms.
Furniture on wheels or with sharp corners.
Slippery socks on a hard floor.
Continuing when your baby is tired.
pull_stand.success: Your baby reaches for the toy and tries to lift their bottom or knees. Standing is a bonus.
ways: Toy on the sofa seat while you sing a short song.
Bare feet on a non-slip floor beside a low table.
Stacking cups on a low table for your baby to reach.

wave.name: Wave bye-bye
wave.why: Waving is one of the first gestures used to communicate. It also teaches turn-taking.
steps: Pick a moment when someone is leaving, or a toy is going to bed.
Face your baby and wave slowly. Say "bye-bye" in a calm voice.
Gently hold your baby's hand and wave it with yours.
Stop and wait for 5 seconds. Let your baby try.
Smile and say "bye-bye" again when your baby moves an arm.
avoid: Waving fast so your baby cannot follow.
Expecting a wave on day 1.
Asking your baby to wave for visitors when they are tired or shy.
wave.success: Your baby watches your hand and moves an arm, even a little.
ways: Wave from the window to the postman or a neighbour.
Say "bye-bye, Teddy" at nap time.
Wave bye-bye to the bath water as it drains.

block_cup.name: Block in the cup
block_cup.goal: Puts something in a container, like a block in a cup.
block_cup.why: It trains hand control and teaches that things can go inside other things.
steps: Sit with your baby on the floor. Bring a wide plastic cup and 3 big soft blocks.
Pick up one block. Put it in the cup and say "In".
Hand a block to your baby and put the cup in front of them.
Wait. Praise your baby when the block goes in, even by accident.
Tip the cup out and start again.
avoid: Blocks small enough to fit through a toilet roll tube. Choose bigger ones.
A cup that is narrow or tips over easily.
Moving your baby's hand every time.
block_cup.success: Your baby holds a block and moves it towards the cup.
ways: Large soft balls into a box.
Wooden spoons into a basket.
Clean socks into a laundry basket.

two_words.name: 2 words together
two_words.goal: Says at least 2 words together, like "More milk."
two_words.why: 2-word phrases are the first step towards sentences.
steps: Pick a moment when your child wants something, such as a snack or a drink.
Wait a moment before you give it. Look at your child.
Say the 2 words yourself, for example "more milk". Keep your voice calm.
Wait 5 seconds. Accept any sound, point or word.
Say the 2 words again as you give it.
avoid: Asking your child to "say it" again and again.
Correcting how the words sound.
Giving the item before your child has a chance to try.
two_words.success: Your child points or makes a sound and listens as you say the 2 words.
ways: Meal times: "more banana", "all gone".
Bath time: "wash toes", "big splash".
At the park: "up please", "go slide".

kick_ball.name: Kick a ball
kick_ball.why: Kicking trains balance on one leg while the other swings.
steps: Use a large, light ball, such as a beach ball. Play on flat grass or a clear floor.
Stand 2 steps away and face your child.
Kick the ball slowly and say "Kick".
Roll the ball gently to your child's feet.
Praise any contact with the foot.
avoid: A hard or heavy ball.
Standing too far away.
Holding your child's hands the whole time, which limits balance practice.
kick_ball.success: Your child steps towards the ball and swings a leg, even if the foot misses.
ways: Kick a ball to knock down a tower of cups.
Kick the ball into a laundry basket on its side.
Kick the ball along and follow it around the garden.

beads.name: String large beads
beads.goal: Strings items together, like large beads or pasta.
beads.why: Threading trains finger control and hand-eye coordination.
steps: Sit beside your child at a table, and stay for the whole activity.
Use a shoelace with tape wrapped around one end and a knot at the other.
Show your child how to push the lace through one large bead.
Hand over the lace and one bead. Wait.
Praise each bead that slides on, then count the beads together.
avoid: Beads small enough to fit through a toilet roll tube. Use big ones.
Leaving your child alone with beads or pasta.
Fixing it for your child as soon as it gets hard.
beads.success: Your child pushes the lace through at least one bead.
ways: Large dry pasta tubes on a shoelace.
Big wooden beads on a pipe cleaner.
Short pieces of paper straw on a string.

chat.name: Back-and-forth chat
chat.goal: Chats with you with at least 2 back-and-forth exchanges.
chat.why: Short chats teach listening, turn-taking and new words.
steps: Pick a calm moment, such as after a meal or in the car.
Ask one open question: "What did you play today?"
Wait 5 seconds. Do not fill the silence.
Repeat the answer and add one word. Ask one follow-up question.
Stop after 2 exchanges and say "Thank you for telling me."
avoid: A string of quick questions.
Correcting grammar.
Answering for your child.
chat.success: Your child answers and you go back and forth twice.
ways: Ask what the person in a picture book is doing.
Chat through a puppet or toy at bedtime.
Ask for "one good thing" at dinner.

catch_ball.name: Catch a large ball
catch_ball.goal: Catches a large ball most of the time.
catch_ball.why: Catching trains hand-eye coordination and reaction time.
steps: Use a large, soft ball. Stand 2 steps from your child.
Say "Arms out like a big hug."
Toss the ball gently, underhand, towards their chest.
Praise a hug around the ball, even if it bounces first.
Take 1 step back after 3 catches in a row.
avoid: Throwing high or fast.
Standing too far away.
Stopping the game after a miss. Say "One more try" instead.
catch_ball.success: Your child moves both arms towards the ball.
ways: Catch a balloon first, then a ball.
Let the ball bounce once, then catch it.
Throw the ball into a big basket.

draw_person.name: Draw a person
draw_person.goal: Draws a person with 3 or more body parts.
draw_person.why: Drawing a person shows how your child sees the body, and it builds pencil grip.
steps: Give your child a thick crayon and plain paper.
Say "Draw someone you know."
Ask, for example, "What else does Grandma have?" and wait.
Praise the idea, not the shape. "I see a head and 2 legs."
Ask "What comes next?" and wait.
avoid: Drawing it for your child.
Correcting the proportions.
Asking "What is that?"
draw_person.success: Your child draws a circle and adds at least 1 part.
ways: Draw the family.
Trace around your child's body on big paper, then add the face.
Use stickers for the body parts, then draw the rest.

hop.name: Hop on one foot
hop.why: Hopping builds balance, leg strength and body control.
steps: Choose a flat, clear spot and have your child wear shoes or go barefoot.
Show your child 2 hops on one foot.
Offer your hand, or let your child stand near a wall.
Ask for 1 hop. Then 2, then 3.
Switch feet and cheer every try.
avoid: Slippery socks on a hard floor.
Counting loudly in a way that adds pressure.
Continuing when your child is tired.
hop.success: Your child lifts one foot and balances for 3 seconds, or hops once with support.
ways: Chalk hopscotch.
Stand like a flamingo for 5 seconds.
Hop along a line of tape.

sit_up.name: Sit on their own
sit_up.why: Sitting frees the hands for play and gives your baby a new view of the room. It builds the trunk strength needed for crawling and standing.
steps: Sit your baby on the floor on a soft blanket, with a cushion ring or your legs around them.
Put a toy in front of them, low enough that your baby leans forward on their hands to reach it.
Keep your hands close but let go for a moment.
Count quietly to 3, then support your baby again before they tip over.
Praise each wobbly second, and stop while your baby is still happy.
avoid: Practising on a bed, sofa or table. Your baby could fall off.
Propping your baby with pillows and walking away.
Long sessions. Sitting is hard work for small muscles.
sit_up.success: Your baby sits for a moment with their hands on the floor in front of them.
ways: Between your legs while you read a picture book together.
In the bath, with your hand behind their back.
Facing a baby-safe mirror on the floor.

hand_to_hand.name: Pass it over
hand_to_hand.goal: Moves things from one hand to the other.
hand_to_hand.why: Passing a toy from hand to hand teaches both sides of the body to work together. Your baby learns to hold, look and let go on purpose.
steps: Sit your baby with support, facing you.
Offer a light toy that is easy to grip, such as a soft ring.
When your baby holds it, offer a second toy to the same hand.
Wait. Your baby may move the first toy to the other hand to take the new one.
Smile and say what happened: "Now it is in this hand."
avoid: Toys small enough to fit through a toilet roll tube.
Taking the toy away before your baby has explored it.
Doing it for your baby every time.
hand_to_hand.success: Your baby holds one toy and reaches for the second one.
ways: 2 soft blocks, one for each hand.
A teething ring offered from one side, then the other.
A wooden spoon at meal times.

peekaboo.name: Peekaboo
peekaboo.goal: Smiles or laughs when you play peekaboo.
peekaboo.why: Peekaboo teaches your baby that people come back when they disappear. It also helps with turn-taking, eye contact and shared laughter.
steps: Sit face to face when your baby is rested and fed.
Cover your face with your hands or a light cloth.
Say "Where is Mummy?" or "Where is Daddy?" in a calm voice.
Uncover your face and say "Peekaboo" with a big smile.
Repeat a few times. Let your baby pull the cloth away when they are ready.
avoid: Covering your baby's face with a cloth they cannot pull off easily.
Loud or sudden reveals that startle your baby.
Continuing when your baby looks away.
peekaboo.success: Your baby looks for your face and smiles when it comes back.
ways: Behind a door, peeking round slowly.
Hiding a teddy under a blanket and making it pop out.
During dressing, as the top goes over their head.

hidden_toy.name: Find the hidden toy
hidden_toy.goal: Looks for things they see you hide.
hidden_toy.why: Finding a hidden toy shows your baby understands that things still exist when they are out of sight. This is a big step in thinking and memory.
steps: Show your baby a favourite toy and let them hold it for a moment.
While your baby watches, put it under a cloth or cup.
Ask "Where did it go?" and wait.
If your baby does not look, leave a small part of the toy showing.
Celebrate when your baby lifts the cloth and finds it.
avoid: Hiding the toy without your baby seeing where it goes.
Hiding it too far away for your baby to reach.
Making it harder before the easy version works.
hidden_toy.success: Your baby looks at or pats the cloth where the toy went.
ways: A ball under an upside-down plastic bowl.
A toy hidden in your closed hand. Then open your hand.
A rattle hidden under a blanket, where your baby can still hear it.

first_steps.name: First steps
first_steps.goal: Takes a few steps on their own.
first_steps.why: Walking gives your child a new way to explore. Short, happy practice builds balance and confidence.
steps: Clear a short path on a non-slip floor. Bare feet give the best grip.
Let your child stand holding the sofa or a low table.
Kneel 2 or 3 steps away with open arms or a favourite toy.
Call your child's name and wait. Do not pull them by the hands.
Catch and cheer, even after 1 step. Then let them sit and rest.
avoid: Baby walkers. They do not help your child learn to walk and can cause falls.
Holding both of your child's hands above their head for long walks.
Slippery socks on a hard floor.
first_steps.success: Your child lets go with one hand or takes 1 step towards you.
ways: From one parent to the other, sitting close together.
Pushing a sturdy toy trolley with a weighted base.
Walking along the sofa to reach a toy at the end.

point_show.name: Point and name
point_show.goal: Points to ask for something or to show you something interesting.
point_show.why: Pointing comes before many first words. It shows your child wants to share attention with you.
steps: Pick a moment with something interesting nearby: a bird, a dog or a light.
Point at it yourself and look at it. Say the word: "Dog."
Look back at your child, then at the dog again.
When your child points, name what they point at.
Add one more word: "Big dog."
avoid: Asking "What is that?" again and again like a test.
Handing things over before your child points or tries a sound.
Background TV during the game.
point_show.success: Your child follows where you point and looks at the right thing.
ways: At the window: cars, birds and people.
In a picture book: "Where is the cat?"
At snack time: point to the fruit and name it.

stack_blocks.name: Stack 2 blocks
stack_blocks.goal: Stacks at least 2 small objects, like blocks.
stack_blocks.why: Stacking trains careful hand control and teaches cause and effect, especially when the tower falls down.
steps: Sit at a low table or on a hard floor with 3 big blocks.
Slowly build a tower of 2 while your child watches. Say "Up".
Knock it down together and laugh.
Hand your child one block and hold the bottom block steady.
Praise any block placed on top, even for a second.
avoid: Blocks small enough to fit through a toilet roll tube.
Soft carpet, which makes towers wobble.
Fixing the tower every time it leans.
stack_blocks.success: Your child puts one block on top of another, even if it falls.
ways: Plastic cups, upside down.
Empty food boxes.
Large soft blocks in the bath.

open_cup.name: Drink from an open cup
open_cup.goal: Drinks from a cup without a lid, and may spill sometimes.
open_cup.why: An open cup trains the lips, tongue and hands together. It is also good for the teeth.
steps: Sit your child in a high chair or at a low table.
Use a small, light open cup with a little water in the bottom.
Take a sip from your own cup to show how.
Help your child hold the cup with both hands and tip it slowly.
Take the cup back after a sip and praise the try.
avoid: A full cup, which spills and leads to frustration.
Drinking while walking or running.
Worrying about spills. A bib and a towel are part of the practice.
open_cup.success: Your child holds the cup to their mouth and drinks a little water.
ways: At every meal, with water.
In the bath, pouring and sipping.
Outdoors on a warm day, with a picnic cup.

give_me.name: Give it to me
give_me.goal: Follows one-step directions without gestures, like "Give it to me."
give_me.why: Following a simple request shows your child understands words without any gestures. Understanding comes before speaking.
steps: Sit together with a few toys your child knows by name.
Ask for one toy with words and a gesture: "Give me the ball," with your hand out.
Say thank you and give it back.
Next time, ask with words only and keep your hands still.
Wait 5 seconds. Praise any try, even the wrong toy.
avoid: Long requests with many steps.
Asking when your child is busy with something else.
Correcting sharply when your child brings the wrong toy.
give_me.success: Your child looks at the toy you named.
ways: "Put the sock in the basket" when tidying.
"Give the spoon to daddy" at meal times.
"Find your shoes" before going out.

scribble.name: First scribbles
scribble.why: Scribbling is the start of drawing and writing. It builds grip and hand-eye coordination.
steps: Tape a large sheet of paper to the table so it does not slide.
Give your child one thick, washable crayon.
Make a few marks yourself and say "Look, lines."
Hand over the crayon and let your child make any mark.
Talk about the marks: "Up and down, round and round."
avoid: Small or sharp pencils.
Asking for a picture of something.
Leaving your child alone with crayons, which can go in the mouth.
scribble.success: Your child makes a mark on the paper.
ways: Chalk on the pavement.
A finger in yoghurt on the high chair tray.
Water and a brush on a dry wall outside.

spoon.name: Eat with a spoon
spoon.why: Using a spoon trains hand control and makes your child proud to eat on their own.
steps: Choose a thick food that sticks to the spoon, such as porridge or yoghurt.
Give your child a short, chunky spoon and keep one for yourself.
Load the spoon together, guiding their hand once or twice.
Let your child try alone while you eat with your own spoon.
Accept the mess and praise every spoonful that reaches their mouth.
avoid: Runny soup in the first weeks.
Wiping their face after every bite.
Taking over when it is slow.
spoon.success: Your child dips the spoon and brings it to their mouth.
ways: Yoghurt at breakfast.
Mashed potato at lunch.
Feeding a teddy with a spoon in play.

stairs_up.name: Up the stairs
stairs_up.goal: Walks up a few stairs, with or without help.
stairs_up.why: Climbing stairs trains balance, leg strength and planning each step.
steps: Use a short flight of 2 or 3 steps. Stand one step below your child.
Let your child hold the rail or your hand.
Say "Step, step" as each foot goes up.
Let your child put both feet on each step. That is fine at this age.
Celebrate at the top, then carry or help them down.
avoid: Stairs without a gate when you are not there.
Hurrying your child or pulling them by the arm.
Toys or clutter on the steps.
stairs_up.success: Your child steps up 1 step while holding your hand.
ways: The steps at a playground slide.
A low step outside your home.
A sturdy step stool at home, with you beside it.

jump.name: Jump with both feet
jump.goal: Jumps off the ground with both feet.
jump.why: Jumping builds leg power, balance and coordination, and it is fun to practise together.
steps: Find soft, flat ground such as grass or a play mat.
Show a small jump with both feet. Bend your knees and say "Ready, jump."
Hold both your child's hands and jump together.
Let go and try again side by side.
Cheer any jump, even if one foot leaves the ground first.
avoid: Jumping off high steps or furniture.
Slippery socks on a hard floor.
Counting or timing, which adds pressure.
jump.success: Your child bends their knees and tries to lift off.
ways: Jump like a frog or a bunny.
Jump over a line of tape on the floor.
Jump into a hoop on the grass.

pretend.name: Pretend play
pretend.goal: Uses things to pretend, like feeding a block to a doll as if it were food.
pretend.why: Pretend play builds imagination, language and problem solving. It also helps children understand everyday life.
steps: Set out a teddy, a plate, a cup and a few blocks.
Say "Teddy is hungry." Give Teddy a block as if it were food.
Hand your child a block and ask "What does Teddy want?"
Follow your child's idea, even if it is unusual.
Add one new step: "Now Teddy needs a nap."
avoid: Taking over the story.
Correcting the pretend play: "That is not food."
Too many toys at once.
pretend.success: Your child gives Teddy something to eat or drink.
ways: A tea party with empty cups.
Putting a doll to bed with a cloth blanket.
Playing shops with real fruit and a bag.

book_talk.name: Book talk
book_talk.goal: Names things in a book when you point and ask "What is this?"
book_talk.why: Talking about pictures helps vocabulary grow quickly. It is also a calm time together.
steps: Choose a book with large, clear pictures of everyday things.
Let your child turn the pages, one at a time.
Point to one picture and ask "What is this?"
Wait 5 seconds. If your child does not answer, say the word and move on.
Repeat the word and add one more: "Yes, a red bus."
avoid: Reading every word on the page when your child wants to talk.
Asking about every picture on every page.
Saying "No" to a wrong answer. Just say the right word.
book_talk.success: Your child points to or names one picture.
ways: A photo album of family and pets.
A catalogue or magazine with clear pictures.
Signs and pictures on a walk.

dress_up.name: Put on a jacket
dress_up.goal: Puts on some clothes by themselves, like loose trousers or a jacket.
dress_up.why: Dressing builds independence, body awareness and hand skills. It also makes mornings easier over time.
steps: Choose a loose jacket with a big zip or no fastening.
Lay it on the floor, open, with the hood at your child's feet.
Ask your child to put both arms in the sleeves.
Show your child how to flip the jacket over their head so it slides onto their shoulders.
Praise the try and help with the zip if needed.
avoid: Practising when you are in a hurry.
Tight clothes or small buttons at first.
Taking over as soon as it gets tricky.
dress_up.success: Your child gets one arm into a sleeve alone.
ways: Pull-on trousers after the bath.
Dressing-up clothes in play.
Putting on a hat and scarf before going out.

colours.name: Name the colours
colours.why: Colour words help children describe and sort the world. Sorting is an early maths skill.
steps: Pick 2 colours to start, such as red and blue.
Collect 3 things of each colour from around the home.
Name each one as you hold it: "Red car, blue cup."
Ask your child to put the red things in one pile.
Then ask "What colour is this?" and wait.
avoid: Too many colours at once.
Quizzing during busy moments.
Saying "Wrong". Just say the right colour and carry on.
colours.success: Your child sorts a few things by colour, even without naming them.
ways: Spot red cars on a walk.
Sort socks by colour on laundry day.
Let your child choose the next crayon by its colour.

pour.name: Pour a drink
pour.goal: Pours water or serves food with an adult watching.
pour.why: Pouring trains careful hand control and makes children feel trusted. It is a real skill used every day.
steps: Use a small jug with a little cold water and a stable cup.
Put both on a tray to catch spills.
Show your child how to hold the cup steady with one hand and pour with the other.
Let your child pour slowly and stop when the cup is half full.
Praise careful pouring and hand over a cloth for spills.
avoid: Hot drinks or heavy jugs.
Glass cups or jugs.
Letting your child pour without you there.
pour.success: Your child gets some water into the cup.
ways: Pouring water from a small jug at dinner.
Pouring dry rice or pasta between bowls.
Serving a spoonful of food onto their own plate.

count_ten.name: Count to 10
count_ten.why: Counting out loud is the start of maths. Counting real things teaches your child that each number goes with one thing.
steps: Count 5 real things together, touching each one: steps, spoons or blocks.
Count slowly and clearly up to 10.
Pause on a number and let your child say the next one.
Let your child lead the counting while you touch the things.
Celebrate when you reach 10, then start again with another set.
avoid: Counting fast without touching the things.
Correcting each slip. Just count again together.
Long counting sessions. A few rounds are enough.
count_ten.success: Your child counts to 5 with you while touching the things.
ways: Count the stairs as you walk up.
Count spoons as you lay the table.
Count jumps in the garden.

rhymes.name: Rhyme time
rhymes.goal: Uses or recognises simple rhymes, like bat and cat.
rhymes.why: Hearing rhymes helps children notice the sounds inside words, which supports reading later.
steps: Sing or say a nursery rhyme your child knows.
Stop before the last word of a line and let your child fill it in.
Play "Does it rhyme?": cat and hat, cat and dog.
Ask your child to find a word that rhymes with "ball".
Laugh at silly made-up rhymes too. They count.
avoid: Explaining rules about rhymes.
Turning it into a test.
Long lists of words.
rhymes.success: Your child fills in the missing rhyming word in a song.
ways: Rhymes in the car.
Rhyming books at bedtime.
Make up rhymes with your child's name.

do_buttons.name: Do up a button
do_buttons.why: Buttons train the small muscles of the fingers, which are also used for holding a pencil.
steps: Start with a shirt or cardigan with big buttons, lying flat on the table.
Show your child slowly: push the button halfway through the hole, then pull it through from the other side.
Let your child try the bottom button.
Help hold the fabric if needed.
Move on to buttons on clothes your child is wearing.
avoid: Small or tight buttons at first.
Practising when you are late.
Doing every button for your child.
do_buttons.success: Your child pushes a button partly through the hole.
ways: A teddy's waistcoat or a doll's coat.
Undoing buttons first, which is easier.
A pillowcase with big buttons.

name_letters.name: Letters in my name
name_letters.goal: Writes some letters in their name.
name_letters.why: Writing their own name is meaningful and motivating. It builds pencil grip and teaches letter shapes.
steps: Write your child's name in big letters on a sheet of paper.
Say each letter as you point to it.
Let your child trace the first letter with a finger, then a crayon.
Write the first letter again in dots and let your child join them.
Praise the try and stick the paper on the fridge.
avoid: Insisting on perfect shapes.
Correcting how the pencil is held during the activity.
Writing the whole name every session.
name_letters.success: Your child traces the first letter of their name.
ways: Letters in sand or salt on a tray.
Letters drawn with a finger on a steamy window.
A name label for their own drawings.

take_turns.name: Take turns in a game
take_turns.goal: Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with others.
take_turns.why: Turn-taking games teach patience, rules and coping with losing, which children use with friends and at school.
steps: Choose a short game with simple rules, such as a matching game or an easy dice game.
Explain one rule only: "First me, then you."
Say whose turn it is each time: "Your turn."
Praise waiting: "You waited for your turn. Well done."
Stop after one short round, win or lose, and say "Good game."
avoid: Long games with many rules.
Always letting your child win.
Continuing to play when your child is tired or upset.
take_turns.success: Your child waits for their turn at least once.
ways: Rolling a ball back and forth.
A simple matching card game.
Taking turns to add a block to a tower.

name_turn.name: Turn to your name
name_turn.goal: Looks when you call their name.
name_turn.why: Turning to their name shows your baby is learning that sounds have meaning and that their name belongs to them.
steps: Wait until your baby is calm and busy with a toy.
Move to one side, where your baby cannot see you directly.
Say your baby's name once, in a warm, clear voice.
Wait a few seconds. Smile and wave when your baby turns.
Try from the other side next time.
avoid: Calling their name again and again.
A noisy room with the TV on.
Using their name only when you say no.
name_turn.success: Your baby pauses or moves their eyes towards your voice.
ways: Call from the doorway when you come into the room.
Sing a short song with their name in it.
Play a hiding game behind the sofa and call their name.

babble_back.name: Ba-ba-ba
babble_back.goal: Makes a lot of different sounds like "mamamama" and "bababababa".
babble_back.why: Babbling is practice for the lips and tongue. When you copy the sounds back, your baby learns that talking is a game you play together.
steps: Sit face to face at your baby's eye level.
Wait for a sound, then copy it: "ba-ba-ba".
Pause and let your baby answer.
Add a new sound now and then: "ma-ma-ma", "da-da-da".
Clap or smile when your baby copies a sound.
avoid: Filling every pause with your own talking.
A dummy in their mouth during the game.
Continuing when your baby looks away.
babble_back.success: Your baby makes any sound after you stop.
ways: Animal sounds with a picture book: "moo", "baa".
Sounds in the bath with a toy duck.
Blowing raspberries back and forth.

crawl.name: Crawl to a toy
crawl.goal: Moves across the floor on hands and knees, or in their own way.
crawl.why: Crawling builds strength in the arms, shoulders and hips, and lets your baby explore. Some babies skip crawling and go straight to walking, which is fine.
steps: Lay your baby on their tummy on a clean, safe floor.
Put a favourite toy in front of them, just out of reach.
Lie down facing your baby and call them over.
Let your baby rock, wiggle or scoot. Do not move them forward by hand.
Hand over the toy when your baby gets close, with lots of praise.
avoid: Baby walkers, and long spells in seats or bouncers.
Small objects or cables on the floor nearby.
Stairs without a gate.
crawl.success: Your baby pushes up on hands and knees, or moves a little towards the toy.
ways: A tunnel of cushions to crawl through, with you at the end.
Rolling a ball slowly away for your baby to follow.
Crawling together, with you on your hands and knees too.

pincer.name: Thumb and finger
pincer.goal: Picks things up between thumb and index finger.
pincer.why: The pincer grip is the start of fine finger control, used later for feeding, buttons and drawing.
steps: Sit your baby in the high chair at a meal.
Put 3 or 4 soft pieces of food on the tray, such as cooked pasta or soft banana.
Pick one up slowly with your thumb and finger so your baby sees how.
Let your baby try. Stay close the whole time.
Praise each piece picked up, eaten or not.
avoid: Hard foods, nuts, whole grapes or anything small and round.
Leaving your baby alone while they eat.
Wiping their hands after every piece.
pincer.success: Your baby rakes a piece towards them or pinches it.
ways: Squashed peas or soft pieces of fruit at lunch.
Picking up puffed baby snacks that melt in the mouth, with you watching.
Pulling scarves out of a tissue box.

climb.name: Climb on the sofa
climb.goal: Climbs on and off a sofa or chair without help.
climb.why: Climbing trains strength, planning and safe ways of getting down, which children need at the playground.
steps: Use a low sofa or armchair with a soft rug in front.
Put a toy on the seat and let your child climb up to get it.
Show your child how to get down feet first, with their tummy on the seat.
Say "feet first" every time your child comes down.
Stay within arm's reach, but let your child do the work.
avoid: High furniture, open windows or shelves that can tip.
Lifting your child up every time.
Climbing down head first.
climb.success: Your child gets one knee onto the seat.
ways: A low step at the playground.
Climbing over a pile of cushions.
Getting onto a low bed for a story.

body_parts.name: Where is your nose?
body_parts.goal: Points to at least 2 body parts when you ask.
body_parts.why: Naming body parts builds vocabulary and body awareness, and turns everyday routines into talk time.
steps: Sit face to face. Touch your own nose and say "nose".
Gently touch your child's nose and say "Your nose".
Ask "Where is your nose?" and wait.
Help by touching it together if needed.
Add one new body part a week: eyes, ears, tummy, toes.
avoid: Too many new words at once.
Testing in front of visitors.
Correcting sharply. Just show the right part.
body_parts.success: Your child touches or looks at the right part.
ways: Name body parts in the bath.
Sing a song about head, shoulders, knees and toes.
Point to body parts on a doll or teddy.

wash_hands.name: Wash hands together
wash_hands.goal: Holds out their hands for you to wash, then helps rub and rinse.
wash_hands.why: Hand washing is a healthy habit and a first step towards doing things alone.
steps: Use a sturdy step so your child can reach the sink.
Check the water is warm, not hot.
Put a little soap on your child's hands and rub them together.
Sing a short song while you rub the backs of their hands and between the fingers.
Rinse, then let your child dry their hands with their own towel.
avoid: Hot water from the tap without checking.
Rushing, which turns it into a fight.
Leaving your child alone on the step.
wash_hands.success: Your child holds out their hands under the water.
ways: Before every meal.
After playing outside.
Washing a doll's hands too.

run_stop.name: Run and stop
run_stop.goal: Runs, and stops when you say "Stop".
run_stop.why: Running builds fitness, and stopping on a signal teaches body control. Both matter for safety near roads.
steps: Find a safe open space, such as a park or garden.
Run together a short way, then say "Stop" and freeze.
Say "Go" and run again.
Let your child call "Go" and "Stop" for you.
End with a slow walk and a drink of water.
avoid: Practising near roads or water.
Long races that end in tired tears.
Slippery floors indoors.
run_stop.success: Your child runs a few steps and slows down when you say "Stop".
ways: Play "Red light, green light" with coloured cards.
Run to a tree and back.
Chase bubbles and stop when they pop.

action_words.name: Doggie run
action_words.goal: Says 2 or more words together, with one action word, like "Doggie run".
action_words.why: Action words let children describe what happens. They help children move from naming things to building sentences.
steps: Sit with your child and watch something that moves, such as a dog, a car or a bird.
Say what it does in 2 words: "Car go", "Bird fly".
Ask "What is the dog doing?" and wait.
Repeat your child's words and add one: "Dog runs fast."
Use the same action words again during the day.
avoid: Asking your child to repeat after you.
Correcting grammar.
Long explanations.
action_words.success: Your child says one action word, like "run" or "go".
ways: Describe what Teddy is doing: "Teddy sleeps."
Talk about pictures in a book.
Describe your child's play as it happens: "You jump."

clean_up.name: Clean-up time
clean_up.goal: Follows simple routines when told, like helping to pick up toys at clean-up time.
clean_up.why: Routines help children feel safe and know what comes next. Helping also builds a sense of belonging.
steps: Pick a fixed moment, such as before dinner.
Say "It is clean-up time" the same way each day.
Give one clear job: "Put the blocks in the box."
Do it together the first few times.
Thank your child and name the job: "You put away the blocks."
avoid: Asking your child to tidy everything at once.
Redoing the job in front of your child.
Using clean-up as a punishment.
clean_up.success: Your child puts one toy in the box after you ask.
ways: A clean-up song.
Racing Teddy to fill the box.
Sorting toys by colour into baskets.

name_self.name: Say your name
name_self.goal: Says their first name when asked.
name_self.why: Knowing and saying their own name is part of your child's growing sense of self. It is also useful if they ever need help.
steps: Point to yourself and say "I am Mum" or "I am Dad".
Point to your child and ask "Who are you?"
Wait. If your child does not answer, say their name together.
Ask a teddy or a puppet the same question for fun.
Praise any try at the name.
avoid: Asking in front of strangers when your child is shy.
Making it a test.
Answering for your child straight away.
name_self.success: Your child points to themselves or says part of their name.
ways: Name labels on drawings.
A photo album: "Who is this?"
Pretend phone calls: "Hello, who is speaking?"

circle.name: Draw a circle
circle.goal: Draws a circle when you show how.
circle.why: Circles are the base for drawing faces, suns and later letters. Copying a shape trains careful hand control.
steps: Tape a large sheet of paper to the table.
Draw a big circle slowly while your child watches. Say "round and round".
Hand over a thick crayon and ask your child to make one too.
Praise any round line, even if it does not close.
Turn it into a sun or a face together.
avoid: Holding your child's hand to draw it for them.
Small paper and thin pencils.
Pointing out what is wrong with the shape.
circle.success: Your child makes a curved line.
ways: Circles in sand with a stick.
Tracing around a cup.
Painting circles with a brush and water outside.

fork.name: Eat with a fork
fork.why: Using a fork trains hand control and lets your child join family meals on equal terms.
steps: Give your child a short, child-sized fork with blunt tips.
Serve foods that are easy to stab, such as cooked carrot or pasta.
Show how to hold the plate steady with the other hand.
Let your child try, and eat with your own fork at the same time.
Praise each bite that reaches their mouth.
avoid: Sharp adult forks.
Slippery foods in the first weeks.
Taking over when it is slow.
fork.success: Your child stabs one piece and brings it to their mouth.
ways: Fruit pieces at snack time.
Feeding a teddy with a toy fork.
Picking up play dough pieces with a fork.

open_lid.name: Twist and open
open_lid.goal: Uses their hands to twist things, like unscrewing lids.
open_lid.why: Twisting uses both hands together in different ways and strengthens the wrist.
steps: Hide a small toy in a plastic jar with a screw lid.
Show how to hold the jar with one hand and twist with the other.
Loosen the lid a little first.
Let your child twist it off and find the toy.
Close it again together and swap roles.
avoid: Glass jars.
Containers that held medicine or cleaning products.
Lids screwed on too tight.
open_lid.success: Your child turns the lid a little.
ways: Opening a snack box.
Turning taps on a toy kitchen.
Screwing nuts onto a big toy bolt.

my_day.name: Tell me about your day
my_day.goal: Talks about at least one thing that happened during the day.
my_day.why: Talking about the day trains memory, order and storytelling, and keeps you close as your child spends more time away.
steps: Pick a calm moment, such as dinner or bath time.
Start with your own short story: "Today I saw a big dog."
Ask one open question: "What did you play today?"
Wait. Repeat what your child says and add one question.
Thank your child for telling you.
avoid: Yes or no questions such as "Was it nice?"
Asking straight after pick-up, when your child is tired.
Correcting the details.
my_day.success: Your child names one thing from the day.
ways: Look at a photo from the day and talk about it.
Ask about the best and the funniest part.
Ask their teddy about its day first.

what_next.name: What comes next?
what_next.goal: Says what comes next in a well-known story.
what_next.why: Predicting what comes next shows your child understands the order of events, a key skill for reading.
steps: Choose a story your child knows well.
Read it as usual, then pause before a big moment.
Ask "What happens next?" and wait.
Praise the answer, even if it is a new idea.
Turn the page together and see.
avoid: New books for this game. Use favourites.
Rushing to read the answer.
Saying "No, that is wrong."
what_next.success: Your child says or shows one thing that happens next.
ways: Pause in songs your child knows.
Retell a story with toys.
Talk through the steps of a routine: "After the bath comes..."

helper.name: Little helper
helper.goal: Likes to help with simple jobs at home.
helper.why: Real jobs build confidence, hand skills and a feeling of being needed in the family.
steps: Pick one safe job, such as putting spoons on the table.
Show it once, slowly.
Let your child do it the whole way, even if it is slow.
Say thank you and name the job.
Keep the same job for a week before adding a new one.
avoid: Jobs with knives, heat or cleaning products.
Fixing the result in front of your child.
Giving jobs as a punishment.
helper.success: Your child finishes part of the job.
ways: Watering plants with a small can.
Putting washing into the machine.
Carrying a light bag of shopping.

crayon_grip.name: Hold the crayon like a pencil
crayon_grip.goal: Holds a crayon or pencil between fingers and thumb, not in a fist.
crayon_grip.why: A finger grip gives better control for drawing and later writing.
steps: Break a crayon into short pieces. Short pieces make a finger grip easier.
Show your own grip: thumb and first finger pinch, middle finger underneath.
Let your child draw anything they like.
If they use a fist, offer the short piece again without comment.
Praise the drawing, not the grip.
avoid: Forcing the fingers into place.
Long writing tasks.
Thin pencils too early.
crayon_grip.success: Your child holds a short crayon with their fingertips for a moment.
ways: Chalk pieces on the pavement.
Painting with a short brush.
Picking up pom-poms with child-safe tweezers, with you watching.

walk_line.name: Walk the line
walk_line.goal: Walks along a line on the floor without stepping off.
walk_line.why: Walking a line trains balance and focus, which help with climbing, cycling and sport.
steps: Put a long strip of tape on the floor, or use a line on the pavement.
Walk along it slowly with your arms out like a plane.
Let your child follow, holding your hand at first.
Let go and count the steps on the line.
Try walking backwards or on tiptoe when it gets easy.
avoid: Raised kerbs or walls.
Slippery socks.
Turning it into a race.
walk_line.success: Your child takes 3 steps on the line.
ways: Walk a rope laid on the grass.
Follow the lines of floor tiles.
Balance a soft toy on their head while walking.

tell_story.name: Tell a story
tell_story.goal: Tells a story they heard or made up, with at least 2 events.
tell_story.why: Storytelling builds vocabulary, memory and the sense of beginning, middle and end needed for reading and writing.
steps: Start a story with one line: "Once there was a cat..."
Ask "What happened next?" and wait.
Add one line of your own, then let your child continue.
Ask "And how did it end?"
Write the story down and read it back at bedtime.
avoid: Taking over with long parts of your own.
Correcting the logic of the story.
Expecting a long story the first time.
tell_story.success: Your child adds one event to the story.
ways: Tell a story with toys or puppets.
Draw a picture, then tell its story.
Retell a favourite book in their own words.

letters_know.name: Name the letters
letters_know.goal: Names some letters when you point to them.
letters_know.why: Knowing letter names and sounds is a step towards reading, and children love spotting letters around them.
steps: Start with the letters in your child's name.
Point to one letter and say its name and sound.
Ask your child to find the same letter on a sign or in a book.
Point and ask "Which letter is this?" and wait.
Stop after a few letters while it is still fun.
avoid: Flash card drills.
All 26 letters at once.
Pressure before school starts.
letters_know.success: Your child finds the first letter of their name.
ways: Letter hunting on a walk.
Fridge magnets.
Letters on food packets in the kitchen.

time_words.name: Yesterday and tomorrow
time_words.goal: Uses words about time, like yesterday, tomorrow, morning or night.
time_words.why: Time words help children plan, remember and understand routines.
steps: Use time words in daily talk: "This morning we went to the park."
At bedtime, ask "What did we do today?"
Then ask "What will we do tomorrow?"
Use a simple picture calendar on the fridge.
Praise any time word your child uses.
avoid: Clock times and hours. They come later.
Correcting each mix-up.
Long lists of plans.
time_words.success: Your child uses one time word correctly.
ways: Count the sleeps until a birthday.
Talk about photos from yesterday.
Use pictures of the morning and night routine.

match_socks.name: Match the socks
match_socks.goal: Does simple chores at home, like matching socks.
match_socks.why: Matching teaches your child to notice details and sort things, and a real chore builds pride.
steps: Put 5 pairs of clean socks in a pile.
Hold up one sock and ask "Where is its partner?"
Let your child search and match the pairs.
Fold or roll each pair together.
Carry them to the drawer together.
avoid: Too many pairs at once.
Socks that look almost the same at the start.
Redoing the pairs in front of your child.
ways: A matching card game.
Matching shoes by the door.
Sorting spoons and forks.

freeze_dance.name: Freeze dance
freeze_dance.goal: Sings, dances or acts for you, and stops when the music stops.
freeze_dance.why: Dancing is great active play. Freezing when the music stops trains listening and self-control.
steps: Clear a safe space and put on a favourite song.
Dance together. Use big moves: jump, spin, wave.
Stop the music and freeze like a statue.
Start again. Let your child stop the music next time.
End with a slow song to calm down.
avoid: Hard corners or slippery floors nearby.
Making anyone leave the game.
Very loud music close to the ears.
freeze_dance.success: Your child stops moving for a moment when the music stops.
ways: Freeze in an animal pose.
Dance with scarves or ribbons.
Put on a little show for the family.

smile_back.name: Smile time
smile_back.goal: Smiles when you talk to or smile at them.
smile_back.why: A smile back is your baby's first way of joining a conversation. It builds the bond between you.
steps: Hold your baby about 20 to 30 cm from your face, the distance a newborn sees best.
Look into your baby's eyes and smile.
Talk in a soft, sing-song voice.
Wait. Give your baby time to answer with a look or a smile.
Give a big smile back when your baby smiles.
avoid: Trying when your baby is hungry or tired.
A busy, noisy room.
Looking at your phone during the game.
smile_back.success: Your baby looks at your face for a few seconds.
ways: During feeds, when your baby looks up at you.
During nappy changes.
Lying side by side on the bed, face to face.

push_up.name: Push up on the arms
push_up.goal: Pushes up onto their elbows or forearms when lying on their tummy.
push_up.why: Pushing up builds the arm and shoulder strength your baby needs to roll, sit and crawl.
steps: Lay your baby on their tummy on a blanket on the floor.
Lie down in front of them, face to face.
Hold a bright toy a little above your baby's eye level.
Move the toy slowly upwards so your baby lifts their chest to follow it.
Praise each push, and turn your baby over when they get tired.
avoid: Practising straight after a feed.
Leaving your baby alone on their tummy.
Soft surfaces such as a bed or sofa.
push_up.success: Your baby lifts their chest for a moment, resting on their forearms.
ways: On your chest while you lie back.
With a baby-safe mirror in front.
With a rolled towel under their chest for support.

laugh.name: Make me laugh
laugh.goal: Chuckles or laughs when you try to make them laugh.
laugh.why: Laughing together is joyful and teaches your baby that sharing feelings is fun.
steps: Pick a time when your baby is awake and happy.
Make a funny sound, such as a gentle "boo" or a raspberry.
Wait and watch your baby's face.
Repeat what made your baby smile, a little bigger.
Stop before your baby gets over-excited.
avoid: Loud or sudden noises that may frighten them.
Tickling for a long time.
Continuing when your baby turns away.
laugh.success: Your baby smiles or squeals at your game.
ways: Gentle tummy kisses.
Funny faces in the mirror.
Lifting your baby gently up and down while you say "Whee".

bang_together.name: Bang the blocks
bang_together.why: Banging 2 toys together teaches cause and effect, and uses both hands at the same time.
steps: Sit your baby up with support and give them 2 big blocks or 2 wooden spoons.
Bang your own 2 blocks together and say "Bang, bang".
Put one block in each of your baby's hands.
Wait and let your baby try.
Cheer and copy your baby's rhythm.
avoid: Small or sharp toys.
Very loud objects close to their ears.
Taking the toys away too quickly.
bang_together.success: Your baby holds one toy in each hand and moves them.
ways: A wooden spoon on a pan.
2 plastic cups.
Clapping hands to music.

arms_up.name: Up, up
arms_up.goal: Lifts their arms up to be picked up.
arms_up.why: Lifting their arms is one of the first ways your baby asks for something without words.
steps: Before you pick your baby up, stop in front of them.
Hold your arms out and say "Up?"
Wait a few seconds for your baby to reach up.
Pick your baby up and say "Up you come".
Do the same every time, so your baby learns the sign.
avoid: Always picking your baby up without a pause.
Waiting so long that your baby gets upset.
Asking when your baby is crying hard.
arms_up.success: Your baby looks up at you or moves their arms.
ways: After a nap in the cot.
After floor play.
Getting out of the bath.

cruise.name: Walk along the sofa
cruise.why: Walking along furniture trains balance and the stepping movement before walking alone.
steps: Let your baby stand holding on to a sturdy sofa.
Put a favourite toy a little way along the seat.
Call your baby to come and get it.
Let your baby side-step along. Stay close, but do not hold them.
Move the toy a bit further next time.
avoid: Furniture that can tip or slide.
Sharp table corners nearby.
Baby walkers.
cruise.success: Your baby takes 1 side step while holding on.
ways: From the sofa to a low table close by.
Along the side of the bed, with you right there.
Pushing a sturdy toy trolley.

stand_alone.name: Stand on their own
stand_alone.goal: Stands without holding on, for a few seconds.
stand_alone.why: Standing alone shows good balance and leg strength, the last step before walking.
steps: Let your baby stand holding your hands, on a soft rug.
Slowly loosen your grip.
Count "1, 2, 3" while your baby balances.
Hold your baby again before a wobble turns into a fall.
Cheer and let your baby sit down gently.
avoid: Hard floors without a rug.
Pulling your baby up by the arms.
Long practice. A few tries are enough.
stand_alone.success: Your baby lets go with one hand while standing.
ways: Hand your baby a toy while they lean on the sofa.
Stand in front of a mirror together.
Dance to a song while your baby stands holding one of your fingers.

pat_a_cake.name: Clapping games
pat_a_cake.goal: Plays games with you, like pat-a-cake.
pat_a_cake.why: Clapping games combine words, rhythm and movement, and teach turn-taking.
steps: Sit face to face.
Sing a short clapping rhyme and clap slowly.
Gently clap your child's hands together with yours.
Pause before the end and wait for your child to clap.
Repeat the same rhyme on other days.
avoid: Changing the rhyme every time.
Clapping too fast to follow.
Holding your child's hands when they pull away.
pat_a_cake.success: Your child moves their hands when you pause.
ways: Clap along to music.
"Round and round the garden" on their palm.
Clap each time a block goes on a tower.

walk_alone.name: Walk across the room
walk_alone.goal: Walks without holding on to anyone or anything.
walk_alone.why: Walking alone gives freedom to explore and builds balance for running and climbing.
steps: Clear a path across the room. Bare feet grip best indoors.
Stand on the other side and call your child.
Hold a toy or open your arms.
Step back a little each time your child reaches you.
Celebrate each walk, short or long.
avoid: Baby walkers.
Slippery socks or floors.
Holding your child's hands up high for long walks.
walk_alone.success: Your child takes 3 steps on their own.
ways: Carrying a light toy across the room.
Walking to put a sock in the basket.
Walking on grass at the park.

finger_feed.name: Feed yourself
finger_feed.goal: Uses their fingers to feed themselves.
finger_feed.why: Feeding themselves trains the fingers and helps children learn when they are full.
steps: Sit your child upright in a high chair. Always stay with them while they eat.
Offer soft finger foods about the size of your finger.
Eat together so your child can copy you.
Let your child pick up food and bring it to their mouth on their own.
Accept the mess and praise the effort.
avoid: Hard foods, whole nuts, and whole grapes or cherry tomatoes. Cut small round foods lengthways into quarters.
Letting your child eat while they walk or play.
Wiping their face after every bite.
finger_feed.success: Your child picks up a piece and brings it to their mouth.
ways: Soft cooked carrot sticks.
Pieces of banana or soft pear.
Toast fingers.

push_car.name: Push the car
push_car.goal: Plays with toys in a simple way, like pushing a toy car.
push_car.why: Using a toy the right way shows your child understands what things are for.
steps: Sit on the floor with a toy car.
Push the car slowly and say "Brmm, brmm".
Push it to your child and say "Your turn".
Wait. Cheer when the car rolls back.
Make a little road with a strip of tape.
avoid: Toys with small parts that come off.
Showing too many toys at once.
Taking over the game.
push_car.success: Your child moves the car on the floor.
ways: A ball rolled back and forth.
A toy pram for a teddy.
A toy phone held to the ear.

help_dress.name: Arm in the sleeve
help_dress.goal: Helps you dress them by pushing an arm through a sleeve or lifting a foot.
help_dress.why: Helping with dressing teaches body awareness and is the first step to dressing alone.
steps: Pick a calm moment, not when you are in a hurry.
Hold the sleeve open and say "Arm in".
Wait for your child to push their arm through.
Do the same with trousers: "Foot up".
Praise every bit of help.
avoid: Dressing in a rush.
Tight clothes.
Doing it all for your child out of habit.
help_dress.success: Your child pushes one arm into a sleeve.
ways: Pyjamas at bedtime.
Jacket before going out.
Socks after the bath.

copy_chores.name: Little sweeper
copy_chores.goal: Copies you doing chores, like sweeping with a broom.
copy_chores.why: Copying everyday jobs is how toddlers learn. It also makes them feel part of the family.
steps: Give your child a small brush or cloth.
Do a simple job next to them, such as wiping a table.
Say what you are doing: "Wipe, wipe."
Let your child copy in their own way.
Thank your child for helping.
avoid: Cleaning products or sprays near your child.
Redoing the job in front of them.
Expecting a clean result.
copy_chores.success: Your child moves the cloth or brush like you.
ways: Sweeping leaves outside.
Wiping the high chair tray.
Putting washing in the basket.

blow_kiss.name: Blow a kiss
blow_kiss.goal: Uses gestures like blowing a kiss or nodding yes.
blow_kiss.why: Gestures help children say what they mean before they have all the words.
steps: When someone leaves, blow a kiss and say "Bye bye, kiss".
Nod your head when you say "Yes".
Shake your head when you say "No".
Wait and give your child time to copy.
Smile and answer the gesture as if it were a word.
avoid: Asking your child to blow a kiss to visitors when they are shy.
Too many new gestures at once.
Correcting how the gesture looks.
ways: Blow kisses to grandparents on a video call.
Nodding yes when you offer a snack.
Thumbs up after a job well done.

throw_ball.name: Throw into a basket
throw_ball.goal: Throws a ball into a basket from a short distance.
throw_ball.why: Throwing trains aim, arm strength and coordination of the whole body.
steps: Put a laundry basket on the floor, 1 big step away.
Use soft balls or rolled-up socks.
Show a slow throw into the basket.
Let your child throw. Move closer if it is too hard.
Step back a little when 3 throws go in.
avoid: Hard balls indoors.
Throwing near windows or faces.
Counting misses.
throw_ball.success: Your child throws a ball towards the basket.
ways: Throw bean bags into a hoop.
Throw a ball to each other in the park.
Throw socks into the laundry basket.

two_step.name: 2 things to do
two_step.goal: Follows 2-step instructions like "Put the toy down and close the door."
two_step.why: Remembering 2 steps trains listening and memory, which children use every day at home and at nursery.
steps: Get your child's attention first. Say their name and wait for eye contact.
Give 2 simple steps: "Take your shoes and put them by the door."
Wait. Repeat once if needed.
Help with the second step if your child stops after the first.
Thank your child and name what they did.
avoid: 3 or more steps at once.
Calling from another room.
Asking when your child is busy playing.
two_step.success: Your child does the first step.
ways: "Wash your hands and come to the table."
"Pick up Teddy and give him to me."
"Find your hat and put it on."

find_colour.name: Find the red one
find_colour.goal: Shows they know at least one colour, like pointing to a red crayon when you ask.
find_colour.why: Knowing a colour is the first step to sorting and describing things.
steps: Pick one colour for the week, such as red.
Point out red things during the day: "Red apple, red car."
Put a red crayon and a blue crayon on the table.
Ask "Which one is red?" and wait.
Praise a right answer. Otherwise show the red one and carry on.
avoid: Many colours at once.
Quizzing all day long.
Saying "Wrong".
find_colour.success: Your child picks up the red one when there are 2 to choose from.
ways: Find red cars on a walk.
Sort red and blue blocks.
Pick red fruit at the shop.

shoes_off.name: Shoes and socks off
shoes_off.goal: Takes some clothes off alone, like shoes, socks or loose trousers.
shoes_off.why: Undressing comes before dressing. It builds independence and hand strength.
steps: Undo the shoe straps or loosen the laces first.
Show how to pull the shoe off at the heel.
Let your child pull their socks off from the toes.
Give them time and wait. Help only if they ask.
Ask your child to put their shoes by the door.
avoid: Practising when you are late.
Tight shoes or boots.
Doing it for your child out of habit.
shoes_off.success: Your child pulls off one sock alone.
ways: At the door after a walk.
Before the bath.
Taking off a hat and gloves.

turn_pages.name: Turn the pages
turn_pages.goal: Turns book pages one at a time when you read together.
turn_pages.why: Turning one page at a time trains small finger movements and makes your child an active reader.
steps: Choose a book with thick card pages first.
Let your child hold the book and turn each page.
Read a line or talk about the picture on each page.
When 2 pages turn together, separate them and let your child try again.
Move to paper pages when card pages are easy.
avoid: Turning the pages for your child.
Rushing to the end.
Thin pages that tear easily at the start.
turn_pages.success: Your child turns one thick page.
ways: Lift-the-flap books.
A photo album with family pictures.
A catalogue to flip through.

play_together.name: Play together
play_together.goal: Notices other children and joins them to play.
play_together.why: Playing with others teaches sharing, waiting and making friends.
steps: Invite one child to play, or go to a playground.
Bring 2 of the same toy to avoid fights over one.
Start a simple game for both, such as rolling a ball.
Step back once the children are playing together.
Help with words when they disagree: "Can I have a turn, please?"
avoid: Long playdates that end in tears.
Forcing your child to share a special toy.
Big groups for a first try.
play_together.success: Your child plays next to another child.
ways: Playing in a sandpit.
Blowing bubbles for both children.
A short dance party.

ask_why.name: Who, what, where?
ask_why.why: Questions show curiosity and help children learn about the world. Your answers build their vocabulary.
steps: Ask questions out loud yourself: "Where is the cat going?"
Wonder together: "Why is the road wet?"
When your child asks, answer in 1 or 2 short sentences.
Turn some questions back: "What do you think?"
Praise good questions: "That is a great question."
avoid: Long answers.
Ignoring a question. Say "We can find out later" if you are busy.
Laughing at a question.
ways: Questions about pictures in a book.
Questions on a walk in the park.
A "What is in the bag?" guessing game.

role_play.name: Pretend roles
role_play.goal: Pretends to be something else during play, like a teacher, a superhero or a dog.
role_play.why: Role play builds imagination, language and empathy, as children try out other points of view.
steps: Offer a few simple props, such as a hat, a bag or a cloth.
Suggest a role: "Shall we play shop?"
Let your child choose who to be.
Play the role your child gives you.
Follow your child's story, even if it changes a lot.
avoid: Directing the whole game.
Correcting the story.
Screens during play.
role_play.success: Your child takes on a role for a short while.
ways: Doctor with a teddy as the patient.
A pretend café with play food.
Animals: walk and sound like a dog or a cat.

comfort.name: Kind words
comfort.goal: Comforts others who are hurt or sad, like hugging a crying friend.
comfort.why: Noticing and caring about how others feel is the basis of friendship and kindness.
steps: Name feelings in daily life: "Teddy looks sad."
Ask "What could we do to help Teddy feel better?"
Act it out together: a hug, a blanket, kind words.
When someone is upset in real life, show what you do and say.
Say when you notice kindness: "You helped your friend. That was kind."
avoid: Forcing a hug or a sorry.
Long lectures.
Laughing at someone who is upset.
comfort.success: Your child suggests one way to help Teddy.
ways: Talk about feelings in a picture book.
Make a get-well drawing for someone.
A feelings game with faces: happy, sad, angry.

four_words.name: Longer sentences
four_words.goal: Says sentences with 4 or more words.
four_words.why: Longer sentences let children explain ideas, needs and feelings clearly.
steps: Listen to what your child says.
Repeat it back with 1 or 2 words added: "Car go" becomes "The car goes."
Ask open questions that need more than one word.
Wait patiently for the answer.
Show interest in what your child says, not in how they say it.
avoid: Asking your child to repeat a sentence correctly.
Finishing sentences for them.
Yes or no questions only.
four_words.success: Your child says a sentence with 3 words.
ways: Describe pictures together.
Talk about what you are cooking.
Tell Teddy what happened today.

sing_song.name: Sing along
sing_song.goal: Says some words from a song, story or nursery rhyme.
sing_song.why: Songs and rhymes help children remember words and hear the rhythm of language.
steps: Choose one short song and sing it every day this week.
Add hand movements to the words.
Leave out the last word of a line and wait.
Let your child fill it in, then keep singing together.
Let your child choose the next song.
avoid: A new song every day.
Singing too fast.
Correcting the words while singing.
sing_song.success: Your child sings or says one word of the song.
ways: Songs in the car.
A bedtime song.
A tidy-up song.

what_for.name: What is it for?
what_for.goal: Answers simple questions like "What is a coat for?" or "What is a crayon for?"
what_for.why: Explaining what things are for builds thinking and vocabulary, and helps your child describe things.
steps: Hold up an everyday object, such as a cup.
Ask "What is a cup for?" and wait.
Praise any answer that makes sense.
Swap roles. Let your child ask you.
Give a silly answer sometimes and let your child correct you.
avoid: Too many questions in a row.
Objects your child does not know.
Correcting each word.
what_for.success: Your child shows how the object is used.
ways: At breakfast: spoon, bowl, napkin.
Getting dressed: coat, hat, gloves.
In the bath: soap, towel, sponge.

unbutton.name: Undo a button
unbutton.why: Undoing buttons trains the fingertips and comes before doing them up.
steps: Lay a cardigan or shirt with big buttons on the table.
Show slowly how to push the button back through the hole.
Let your child try the bottom button.
Hold the fabric if needed.
Praise the effort and move on to the next button.
avoid: Small or tight buttons.
Practising when you are late.
Doing it for your child.
unbutton.success: Your child pushes a button partly through the hole.
ways: A doll's or teddy's coat.
A pillowcase with big buttons.
Their own cardigan at bedtime.

one_foot.name: Stand on one foot
one_foot.goal: Balances on one foot for a few seconds.
one_foot.why: Balancing on one foot builds strength and control, needed for hopping, kicking and climbing.
steps: Stand face to face on a flat, safe floor.
Lift one foot and say "Flamingo".
Let your child copy, holding your hand at first.
Count slowly together.
Swap feet and try again.
avoid: Slippery socks.
Hard corners nearby.
Competitions that end in frustration.
one_foot.success: Your child lifts one foot for a moment.
ways: Stand like a flamingo while brushing teeth.
Freeze on one foot in a dance game.
Balance while putting on trousers, holding the wall.

scissors.name: Snip with scissors
scissors.why: Cutting uses both hands in different ways and strengthens the hand for drawing and writing.
steps: Use child-safe scissors with rounded tips. Stay with your child the whole time.
Show how the thumb goes on top: "Thumb up, open, close."
Hold a strip of thick paper for your child.
Let your child snip small pieces off the strip.
Collect the pieces and glue them into a picture.
avoid: Adult scissors.
Walking around with scissors.
Thin paper that bends.
scissors.success: Your child opens and closes the scissors.
ways: Snip play dough snakes.
Cut straws into beads.
Snip fringes on a paper strip.

balance_bike.name: Balance bike
balance_bike.goal: Rides a balance bike, pushing along with their feet.
balance_bike.why: A balance bike teaches balance and steering, and makes learning to cycle easier later.
steps: Choose a bike where your child can sit with both feet flat on the ground.
Always make sure your child wears a helmet.
Start on a flat, quiet path away from roads.
Let your child walk with the bike between their legs, then push and glide.
Celebrate short glides with their feet up.
avoid: Roads, slopes and steps.
Riding without a helmet.
Holding the bike all the time.
balance_bike.success: Your child walks the bike a few steps while sitting.
ways: A park path.
Riding to a tree and back.
Following you on a short loop.

numbers_five.name: Spot the numbers
numbers_five.goal: Names some numbers between 1 and 5 when you point to them.
numbers_five.why: Knowing what numbers look like helps with counting, games and later maths at school.
steps: Write the numbers 1 to 5 in big print on paper.
Point to one and say its name.
Put the same number of objects next to it.
Point and ask "Which number is this?"
Look for numbers around you: doors, buses, clocks.
avoid: All the numbers at once.
Flash card drills.
Pressure before school.
ways: House numbers on a walk.
A dice game.
Numbers in the lift.

craft.name: Craft time
craft.goal: Pays attention for 5 to 10 minutes during an activity like arts and crafts.
craft.why: Staying with one activity for a few minutes trains focus, which children need at school. Screen time does not count.
steps: Set out a simple craft: paper, glue stick, crayons and a few shapes.
Give one idea: "Shall we make a card for Grandma?"
Sit with your child and make your own.
Praise focus: "You worked on that for a long time."
Hang the finished work where everyone can see it.
avoid: Too many materials at once.
Finishing the craft for your child.
Screens in the background.
craft.success: Your child stays with the craft for a few minutes.
ways: Leaf pictures with glue.
Play dough shapes.
Sticker scenes.

story_questions.name: What happened in the story?
story_questions.goal: Answers simple questions about a book or story after you read it.
story_questions.why: Talking about a story after reading builds understanding, memory and early reading skills.
steps: Read a short story together.
Ask one easy question: "Who was in the story?"
Ask one more: "What did the bear do?"
Ask a feeling question: "How did the bear feel?"
Let your child look back at the pictures to find the answer.
avoid: Many questions after every page.
Turning reading into a test.
Saying "No" to a wrong answer. Look at the page together instead.
ways: Talk about a film you watched together.
Retell what happened during a family visit.
Ask about a song's story.

long_chat.name: Keep the chat going
long_chat.goal: Keeps a conversation going with more than 3 back-and-forth exchanges.
long_chat.why: Longer conversations build vocabulary, listening and the skill of staying on a topic.
steps: Pick a topic your child loves, such as dinosaurs or a friend.
Ask an open question and listen fully.
Answer with interest and ask one more question.
Share something of your own about the topic.
Count the turns together for fun.
avoid: Questions with yes or no answers.
Looking at your phone during the chat.
Changing the topic too quickly.
long_chat.success: You go back and forth 3 times.
ways: A walk with no phone.
Dinner table chat.
Bedtime chat in the dark.

clear_table.name: Clear the table
clear_table.goal: Does simple chores at home, like clearing the table after eating.
clear_table.why: Regular small jobs build responsibility, hand skills and pride.
steps: After a meal, give one job: "Please bring your plate to the kitchen."
Show how to carry it with both hands.
Let your child carry it alone, slowly.
Thank your child.
Add one more item, such as a cup, next week.
avoid: Glass or heavy plates.
Sharp knives on the plate.
Expecting perfect results.
clear_table.success: Your child carries their own plate.
ways: Putting cups in the sink.
Wiping the table with a cloth.
Putting napkins in the bin.

bike_stabilisers.name: Pedal a bike
bike_stabilisers.goal: Rides a bike or tricycle using the pedals.
bike_stabilisers.why: Pedalling builds leg strength, coordination and confidence outdoors.
steps: Check the bike fits: your child sits with their feet reaching the pedals easily.
Always make sure your child wears a helmet.
Start on a flat, quiet path away from roads.
Help with the first push, then let your child pedal.
Stay close and praise each pedal turn.
avoid: Roads, slopes and busy paths.
Riding without a helmet.
Long rides that end in tired tears.
bike_stabilisers.success: Your child turns the pedals a full circle.
ways: A loop in the park.
Riding to a friend's house on a quiet path.
Pedal and stop on a signal.

dress_alone.name: Get dressed alone
dress_alone.goal: Gets dressed with little or no help.
dress_alone.why: Dressing alone builds independence and makes mornings smoother over time.
steps: Lay out the clothes the night before, in order.
Show the order once: pants, trousers, top, socks.
Let your child dress alone and wait.
Help only with hard parts, such as a zip.
Praise the effort, not how the outfit looks.
avoid: Practising on busy mornings.
Clothes with many small buttons.
Redressing your child afterwards.
dress_alone.success: Your child puts on 2 items alone.
ways: Pyjamas at night.
Dressing-up clothes in play.
A race against a song.

brush_teeth.name: Brush and check
brush_teeth.goal: Brushes their own teeth, with you finishing off.
brush_teeth.why: Brushing alone builds a healthy habit. Children still need an adult to help until at least age 7.
steps: Put a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste on the brush.
Let your child brush first, using small circles.
Count or sing to keep going for about 2 minutes.
Then brush once more yourself to finish off.
Let your child spit out, without rinsing with water.
avoid: Swallowing the toothpaste.
Skipping the bedtime brush.
Leaving brushing to your child alone.
brush_teeth.success: Your child brushes the front teeth alone.
ways: Brush together in front of the mirror.
A 2-minute brushing song.
A sticker for each evening brush.
