4.summary: Your baby is about 2 mm long, the size of a poppy seed. They float in a small sac of fluid that cushions them, and the cells that will become the placenta are forming. You may look and feel the same as before. Some people notice a missed period, tiredness, sore breasts or feeling sick.
prepare: Contact your doctor or midwife to plan your first check-ups.
Ask which supplements are recommended in early pregnancy, such as folic acid.
Stop smoking and drinking alcohol, and cut down on caffeine. Ask for support if you need it.
If you take regular medicine, do not stop it on your own. Ask your doctor first.
ask: When is my first appointment, and when is the first scan?
Which supplements should I take, and for how long?
Is my regular medicine safe in pregnancy?

5.summary: Your baby is still about 2 mm long, the size of a sesame seed. The brain, spinal cord and heart are forming, and the heart may start to beat around now. The first tiny features of the face are taking shape. You may feel very tired, feel sick at any time of the day, or need to pee more often. Tell your doctor or midwife about any bleeding.
prepare: Rest when you can. Tiredness is common in the first weeks.
Small meals spread through the day can help with feeling sick.
Light activity, such as a short daily walk, is a good start.
Start a list of questions for your first appointment.
ask: What can I do about feeling sick?
Which foods should I avoid?
When should I call you about cramps or spotting?

6.summary: Your baby is about 6 mm long, the size of a pea. Small buds appear that will grow into arms and legs, and there are tiny dents where the ears will be. The brain and liver keep developing. Feeling sick and tired is common now, often worst in the morning.
prepare: Eat small meals and drink regularly through the day.
Tell your doctor or midwife if you cannot keep food or drink down.
Find out about antenatal classes. Many can be done online.
Remember that many people start to feel better after week 12.
ask: When will I have my first scan?
What can help with morning sickness?
Which antenatal classes do you recommend?

7.summary: Your baby is about 10 mm long from head to bottom, the size of a grape. The brain grows fast, so the forehead looks large. The arm buds get longer, and their flat ends will become tiny hands. The amount of blood in your body rises, so you may feel more thirsty.
prepare: Drink regularly through the day.
Stay active. Short daily walks count.
Eat a varied diet. You do not need to eat for two.
Talk to your midwife, doctor or someone you trust if you feel anxious or low.
ask: How much activity is right for me?
Who can I call between appointments?

8.summary: Your baby is about 16 mm long, the size of a raspberry. The placenta is growing into the wall of the womb to bring food and oxygen. The arms are longer than the legs for now. Tiredness, feeling sick and needing to pee more often are still common.
prepare: Your first full appointment with the midwife or doctor often happens in the coming weeks.
Check when your first scan will be.
Tell your doctor about any long-term condition you have.
ask: Which tests and scans will I be offered?
What are my options for where to give birth?
What should I do if I have bleeding or pain?

9.summary: Your baby is about 22 mm long from head to bottom, the size of a strawberry. The face is easier to recognise now, with eyelids, a small mouth and a tongue with tiny taste buds. Hands and feet are developing, and the first bones are starting to form. Pregnancy hormones are at their peak, so tiredness, feeling sick, sore breasts and mood swings are common. These often ease in the coming weeks.
prepare: If your first full appointment is not booked yet, book it now. It often happens between weeks 8 and 12.
You will be offered blood tests and screening. You can ask what each test is for before you decide.
Keep taking the supplements your doctor or midwife recommended.
Tell your doctor or midwife about any bleeding.
ask: Which screening tests are offered, and what do they look for?
How many appointments and scans will I have?

10.summary: Your baby is about 30 mm long, the size of a small apricot, and from now on is called a foetus. Your baby makes small jerky movements that can be seen on a scan, but you will not feel them yet. The ears, upper lip and nostrils are forming, and tiny buds for the milk teeth sit in the jaw. The heart beats about 180 times a minute. Your womb is about the size of a large orange, so trousers may start to feel tight. Bloating, wind and heartburn are common, because hormones relax the muscles of the gut.
prepare: Small meals and a short walk after eating can help with bloating.
Ask when your first scan is, if it is not booked yet. It is often done between weeks 8 and 14.
Looser, comfortable clothes help as your waist changes.
ask: When is my dating scan?
What can I safely take for heartburn?

11.summary: Your baby is about 41 mm long, the size of a fig. Fingers and toes are separating, and tiny nails are forming. The placenta is about to take over feeding your baby. The amount of blood in your body rises by up to half, so you may feel warm, sweaty or dizzy. Aches around the bump are common as muscles and ligaments stretch. Get medical advice for any bleeding or strong pain.
prepare: Stand up slowly if you feel dizzy, and drink regularly.
Gentle activity, such as walking or swimming, can help with tiredness.
At the first scan you may be offered a screening test that measures the fluid at the back of your baby's neck. Ask what the result can and cannot tell you before you decide.
ask: What does the first trimester screening check?
Is it safe to keep doing my usual sport or activity?

12.summary: Your baby is about 5.4 cm long, the size of a plum. All the organs and muscles have formed and will keep growing. The skeleton is starting to harden into bone. Many people have the first scan around now and see the heartbeat. Feeling sick often eases from here, and you may feel hungrier. Your waist may thicken and your breasts may grow.
prepare: Many people tell family, friends or their employer after the first scan. Choose what feels right for you.
Ask your employer about your rights at work during pregnancy.
Start thinking about contraception after the birth. It is easy to forget later.
Write down questions that come up after the scan.
ask: What did the scan show, and when is the next one?
When do I need to tell my employer?

13.summary: Welcome to the second trimester. Your baby is about 7.4 cm long, the size of a peach. Movements become more controlled, and some babies already suck their thumb, which is practice for feeding. As the womb rises out of the pelvis, a small bump may show and you may need to pee less often. Swollen or bleeding gums, nosebleeds, constipation and leg cramps are common.
prepare: Start gentle pelvic floor exercises. A few minutes a day helps prevent leaks later.
Brush your teeth gently and see a dentist. Pregnancy can make gums sore.
Avoid contact with anyone who has chickenpox or rubella, and get advice if you are exposed.
Let someone else clean the cat litter, and avoid undercooked or cured meat, to lower the risk of toxoplasmosis.
ask: How do I do pelvic floor exercises correctly?
Which vaccines are recommended in pregnancy where I live?

14.summary: Your baby is about 8.5 cm long, the size of a kiwi. The head is rounder and more in proportion with the body. Your midwife may be able to hear the heartbeat with a small handheld monitor. Your baby swallows the fluid around them, and the kidneys start to make urine. You may notice yellow stains in your bra. This can be colostrum, the first milk, and is normal.
prepare: If you work, ask your employer to check your tasks for risks in pregnancy.
Water, fibre and daily activity help with constipation.
Keep up gentle activity most days.
ask: Can you listen to the heartbeat at my next visit?
Is the medicine or supplement I take still right for me?

15.summary: Your baby is about 10.1 cm long, the size of an apple. A soft layer of hair called lanugo grows over the body, and eyebrows and eyelashes begin to form. Hearing is starting, so your baby may hear your voice, your heartbeat and the sounds of your tummy. You may feel less steady on your feet, have itchy skin or notice more discharge.
prepare: Talk or sing to your bump if you like. Partners can join in.
See your doctor or midwife if discharge changes, peeing hurts, or itching gets worse, especially at night.
Flat, comfortable shoes help as your balance changes.
ask: Is the discharge I have normal?
What can I do about itchy skin?

16.summary: Your baby is about 11.6 cm long, the size of an avocado. The nervous system now lets the arms and legs move, and the hands can make fists. A growth spurt is coming. A few people feel the first movements from about week 16, but most feel them between weeks 18 and 24, often later in a first pregnancy. Around now you may have a check-up of your blood pressure and urine, and go through your blood test results.
prepare: Test your home carbon monoxide alarm, or get one if you do not have one.
Keep your pregnancy notes and test results together and bring them to every visit.
Do not stop iron or any other medicine without advice, even if it upsets your stomach.
ask: What do my blood test results show?
Is my blood pressure normal?

17.summary: Your baby is about 12 cm long, the size of a pomegranate. The eyes move under closed lids, and your baby reacts to loud noises. Fingernails are growing, and the fingerprints are already unique. You may feel the first movements between weeks 18 and 24, often like bubbles or fluttering. Your waist starts to disappear, and stretch marks may appear. About 1 in 5 pregnant women feel stressed or anxious. Talk to your doctor or midwife if you feel low.
prepare: Start thinking about where you would like to give birth: hospital, birth centre or home, depending on what is available near you.
Share how you feel with someone you trust.
If you work, ask your employer to check that your tasks and breaks are suitable in pregnancy.
ask: Which places to give birth are available near me?
Who can I talk to if I feel anxious?

18.summary: Your baby is about 14.2 cm long, the size of a pepper. Hearing, touch, swallowing and sucking are developing, and the arms and legs wriggle. Your blood pressure may be lower than usual, so standing up fast can make you dizzy. A dark line may appear down your tummy. It usually fades after birth.
prepare: The anomaly scan, which checks how your baby is developing and looks for some physical conditions, often happens between weeks 18 and 21.
Decide if you want to know the sex, and tell the sonographer before the scan starts.
Bring your partner or someone close, if you like.
ask: What does the anomaly scan check?
What happens if the scan finds something?

19.summary: Your baby is about 15.3 cm long, the size of a large tomato. The adult teeth are already forming behind the milk teeth, and your baby is gaining weight. The hormone relaxin loosens your ligaments, so running or long walks may feel uncomfortable. Pelvic pain, leg cramps and heartburn are common.
prepare: Choose gentle activity, such as swimming, walking or pregnancy yoga.
Tell your doctor or midwife about pelvic pain that makes walking or turning in bed hard. Help is available.
Raise any worry with your doctor or midwife. No question is too small.
ask: Is my pelvic pain something to check?
Which exercise is safe for me now?

20.summary: Halfway there. From this week babies are measured from head to heel instead of head to bottom, so the number jumps. Your baby is about 25.6 cm long, the size of a banana. A white, greasy layer called vernix protects the skin. Your baby kicks, punches and turns more often. Leg cramps at night are common.
prepare: The anomaly scan may happen this week, if it has not already.
Ask which vaccines are recommended in pregnancy where you live. Many European countries offer whooping cough, flu and RSV vaccines, mostly from about week 20 to week 36.
Ask your employer which forms you need for maternity leave and pay.
ask: Which vaccines do you recommend for me, and when?
Which forms do I need for maternity leave?

21.summary: Your baby is about 26.7 cm long, the size of a carrot, and now weighs more than the placenta. Your baby practises sucking and breathing and has times of waking and sleeping. Fine hair covers the body, and your baby can hear voices from outside. Your growing bump shifts your balance, and backache is common.
prepare: Bend your knees and keep your back straight when you lift something.
Rest when you can, and nap if you need to.
Ask for a seat on public transport when you need one.
ask: What can help with backache?
Who do I call if something about the scan worries me?

22.summary: Your baby is about 27.8 cm long, the size of a sweet potato. The lungs keep developing, and your baby practises breathing. Taste buds are forming, and what you eat may flavour the fluid around your baby. Stretch marks, piles and indigestion are common now.
prepare: Eat a varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables. You do not need extra food yet.
Plan some rest and things that help you relax.
Get help straight away for severe pain or bleeding.
ask: Is there anything I should eat more of?
What can help with piles?

23.summary: Your baby is about 28.9 cm long, the size of a large mango. The arms and legs are now in proportion. Kicks get stronger, and you may see your bump move. You may leak a little colostrum, and your ribs may ache as your lungs get less room.
prepare: Get to know your baby's usual pattern of movements. If movements slow down or stop, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away. Do not wait until the next day.
Use sun cream and stay in the shade at midday. Dark patches on the skin get darker in the sun during pregnancy.
Swap some tea and coffee for drinks without caffeine.
ask: How do I know if movements are reduced?
Which number do I call outside working hours?

24.summary: Your baby is about 30 cm long, the size of a corn on the cob. Some babies born from now can survive with intensive care in a neonatal unit. You may feel hungrier and gain weight. Aches in the ribs, back and tummy are common as ligaments loosen.
prepare: Many people are offered a blood sugar test for diabetes in pregnancy between weeks 24 and 28.
Start a birth plan: pain relief, who will be with you, and what matters to you.
Think about contraception after the birth.
Talk to your doctor or midwife if you feel anxious or low.
ask: Which pain relief options do I have?
What happens if my baby is born early?

25.summary: Your baby is about 34.6 cm long, the size of a courgette. Your baby is very active, may jump at loud noises and can get hiccups. Swelling in your face, hands or feet is common. Tell your midwife or doctor about it, so they can check your blood pressure.
prepare: Get urgent help for a severe headache, problems with your sight, or pain just below the ribs. These can be signs of pre-eclampsia.
Raise your feet when you sit, and avoid standing for a long time.
If you work, check when you need to give your leave dates to your employer.
ask: Is my swelling normal?
How will you check for pre-eclampsia?

26.summary: Your baby is about 35.6 cm long, the size of a cucumber. The eyes open for the first time, and your baby learns to blink. You may feel clumsy as your balance shifts, and leg cramps may get worse at night. Forgetfulness, often called baby brain, is common.
prepare: Keep learning your baby's pattern of movements. Contact your midwife straight away if movements slow down or stop.
Avoid heavy lifting and take breaks to sit down.
Find out about antenatal classes for both parents.
ask: Which classes do you recommend for us?
What can I do about leg cramps?

27.summary: Your baby is about 36.6 cm long, the size of a cauliflower. The lungs keep developing, and your baby gets plumper as fat fills out the skin. You may snore more and sleep less well. This is the last week of the second trimester.
prepare: Sleep on your side from now on. It is better for blood flow to your baby. Pillows can help.
Check airline rules if you plan to fly. Many ask for a fitness to fly letter later in pregnancy.
Think about where you would like to give birth.
ask: Is it safe for me to travel?
Up to which week can I fly?

28.summary: Welcome to the third trimester. Your baby is about 37.6 cm long, the size of an aubergine. The heart beats about 140 times a minute, faster than yours, and can be heard with a stethoscope. Heartburn, backache and swollen ankles are common. Sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet can be a sign of pre-eclampsia. Call your midwife straight away.
prepare: Ask which vaccines are offered in late pregnancy. Many countries offer RSV and whooping cough vaccines around now, if you have not had them yet.
Plan your baby's sleep space: a cot or crib with a firm, flat, well-fitting mattress.
You only need a little more food from now. You still do not need to eat for two.
Wash your hands often, and wear gloves for gardening and cat litter.
ask: Which vaccines should I have now?
Which checks will my baby have after birth?

29.summary: Your baby is about 38.6 cm long, the size of a butternut squash. Your baby is fully formed. Over the next weeks the organs mature and fat builds up. You may feel breathless, need the toilet more at night, and feel awkward or irritable.
prepare: Think about who your birth partner will be.
Keep doing pelvic floor exercises.
Ask about the checks your baby is offered in the first days after birth.
ask: What should my birth partner know?
What are the signs that labour has started?

30.summary: Your baby is about 39.9 cm long, the size of a cabbage. The eyes can focus now. After birth, your baby will see a face best at about 20 to 25 cm. You may feel breathless on stairs and have vivid dreams.
prepare: Read about the stages of labour, or join a class that covers them.
Get a few baby clothes in newborn size and the next size up. Babies grow fast.
Keep talking about worries with someone you trust.
ask: What happens in each stage of labour?
When should I come to the hospital?

31.summary: Your baby is about 41.1 cm long, the size of a coconut. Your baby moves a lot, sucks their fingers and can recognise voices. Your bump may tighten for 20 to 30 seconds and then relax. These practice contractions are called Braxton Hicks. They are harmless, but call your midwife if they become painful or regular.
prepare: Get a cot, crib or Moses basket with a firm, flat, waterproof mattress. No pillows or duvets for your baby.
If you plan to use a sling or carrier, learn how to use it safely.
Some babies are not head down yet. Most turn on their own before birth.
ask: Is my baby head down?
When should I call you about tightenings?

32.summary: Your baby is about 42.4 cm long, the length of a bunch of celery. Your baby will put on about 1 kg of fat over the next 4 weeks. Most babies are head down by now. Movements continue at the same rate until birth, so a change or drop is a reason to call your midwife straight away. Walking may get harder, and many people start to waddle.
prepare: Choose a pushchair or pram. Check the brakes if it is second hand.
Ask about vitamin K for your baby after birth, so you can decide in advance.
If you have a planned caesarean, ask how long you will stay in hospital and arrange help at home.
ask: What happens if my baby is not head down?
Should my baby have vitamin K, and how is it given?

33.summary: Your baby is about 43.7 cm long, the size of a pineapple. The brain and nervous system keep developing fast. The bones are hardening, but the skull stays soft so your baby's head can pass through the birth canal. You may feel heaviness low in the pelvis.
prepare: Pack your hospital bag, with your notes and birth plan.
Save the maternity unit number and your hospital reference in your phone, and on paper.
Buy a new car seat and practise fitting it before the birth.
ask: What should I pack for me and my baby?
Which entrance and number do I use when labour starts?

34.summary: Your baby is about 45 cm long, the size of a small melon. Your baby lies curled up, with the knees towards the chest. When your baby drops lower into the pelvis, breathing may get easier and heartburn may ease, but you may need to pee more often. Your breasts may feel full and leak colostrum.
prepare: Plan when you would like to start maternity leave.
Keep sleeping on your side.
Go to your check-up this week if one is offered.
ask: Is my baby growing well?
When can I start my leave?

35.summary: Your baby is about 46.2 cm long, the size of a honeydew melon. Your baby gets chubbier, which helps them stay warm after birth. Space is tight, but movements should stay as strong and regular as before. Sore ribs are common with an active baby. Severe pain just below the ribs can be a sign of pre-eclampsia. Get urgent help.
prepare: Ask about testing for group B strep, if it is offered where you live.
Think about pain relief. You can change your mind on the day.
Contact your midwife straight away if movements change or stop.
ask: Will I be tested for group B strep?
Which pain relief can I have where I give birth?

36.summary: Your baby is about 47.4 cm long, the size of a lettuce. The lungs are probably ready to breathe without help, and your baby can suck and digest milk. Your baby may move down into the pelvis. A little pee may leak when you laugh or cough.
prepare: Keep doing pelvic floor exercises, and have maternity pads ready.
If your baby is not head down, ask about turning your baby by hand, called external cephalic version.
Keep your hospital bag by the door.
ask: Is my baby head down?
What are my options if my baby is breech?

37.summary: Your baby is about 48.6 cm long, the length of a leek, and is now considered full term. Your baby practises frowning and smiling and has active and calm times. About 95 in 100 babies are head down now. You may want to clean and prepare your home. This is called nesting.
prepare: Learn the signs of labour: regular contractions, a show of mucus, backache, and waters breaking.
Learn the signs of low mood after birth, for you and your partner.
Stock up on easy meals for the first weeks.
ask: When should I call you once labour starts?
What support is there after the birth?

38.summary: Your baby is about 49.8 cm long, the size of a large cabbage, and could arrive any day. Most of the fine body hair has gone. Your baby stores the first poo, called meconium, in the bowel. It usually passes after birth. Feeling impatient or bored is common now.
prepare: Ask what happens if your pregnancy goes past 41 weeks.
If you plan a home birth, get everything ready.
Rest and save your energy.
ask: What happens if I go past my due date?
When would you suggest induction?

39.summary: Your baby is about 50.7 cm long, the size of a small watermelon. The skin is getting thicker. Your baby may be born covered in vernix, a white waxy layer, or it may have mostly gone. You may notice more discharge, backache and pressure low in the bump. A show, a plug of mucus that can be pink or bloody, can mean labour is near.
prepare: Call your midwife or maternity unit when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every 5 minutes, or if you think your waters have broken.
Get urgent help for bleeding, a severe headache, changes in your sight, sudden, severe swelling, constant tummy pain or a fever.
Contact your midwife straight away if movements slow down or stop.
ask: What happens when I call the maternity unit?
When should I come in?

40.summary: Your baby is about 51.2 cm long, the size of a pumpkin. This is your due week, but only a few babies arrive on the due date itself. Your baby is squashed up, but movements should keep their usual pattern. Lower backache, period-like cramps and practice contractions can all be early signs of labour.
prepare: Contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away if movements slow down or stop.
Call when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every 5 minutes, or when your waters break.
Keep your phone charged and your bag ready.
When your baby arrives, tap Baby arrived on Home and Hoppo switches to baby mode.
ask: What happens if my baby has not arrived by next week?
Which check-ups will I have after my due date?

t01.text: Tired days happen. A 2-minute version of this week's mission still counts.

t02.text: Stop while it is still fun. Ending on a smile makes tomorrow easier.

t03.text: Start small. One mission a week can become a real habit.

t04.text: Praise the try, not the result.

t05.text: Every child has their own pace. Compare with last month, not with other children.

t06.text: Missed a week? Nothing is lost. Pick up where you left off.

t07.text: Babies learn by repeating things. The same game 5 days in a row is a good plan.

t08.text: Talk through what you do: "Now we put on the sock." It all counts as speech practice.

t09.text: Floor time is practice time. A blanket and a toy are enough.

t10.text: Give 2 choices: "Red cup or blue cup?" It builds words and keeps the peace.

t11.text: Wait 5 seconds after a question. Silence gives words room to come.

t12.text: Let your child help with small jobs. Carrying a sock to the basket is a mission too.

t13.text: Ask "What was the best part of today?" at dinner. Short chats add up.

t14.text: Let your child lead the game for 5 minutes. You follow.

t15.text: Mistakes are part of the game. Say "One more try" and keep it light.

t16.text: Write down questions for your next check-up as they come. Bring the list.

t17.text: Put your appointments in the calendar and let Hoppo remind you.

t19.text: Ask someone close to you what help they can offer in the first weeks.

t20.text: You know your child best. Hoppo only gives ideas.

t21.text: Talk or sing to your bump. Your baby starts to hear your voice in the middle of pregnancy.

t22.text: A short walk counts as activity. 10 minutes a day is a good start.

t23.text: Write down how you feel this week. It is lovely to read back later.

t24.text: Ask your partner or a friend to come to one check-up with you.

t25.text: Plan a calm half hour for yourself this week. You matter too.

t26.text: Start a list of names you like. No decision needed yet.

t27.text: Get to know your baby's pattern of movements in the second half of pregnancy.

t28.text: Save the number of your maternity unit in your phone today.

t29.text: Ask a friend who has a baby what helped them most in the first weeks.

t30.text: Small, regular snacks can help on days you feel sick.

t31.text: Side sleeping with a pillow between your knees can feel more comfortable.

t32.text: Pack your hospital bag a few weeks before the due date. Then forget about it.

t33.text: Cook a few extra meals for the freezer in the last weeks.

t34.text: Welcome. Each week Hoppo shows how big your baby is and what to prepare.

t35.text: Tired today? Rest is part of growing a baby.

t36.text: Hold your baby face to face and pull a funny face. Babies love to copy.

t37.text: Describe what your baby looks at. Words come from many small moments.

t38.text: Change the toy now and then. New things keep your baby curious.

t39.text: Lie on the floor next to your baby. The view from down there is different.

t40.text: Sing the same song at bedtime every night. Babies love what they know.

t41.text: Read a picture book together, even if your baby only chews it.

t42.text: A walk outside is good for both of you. Fresh air and new sounds.

t43.text: Pause after you speak. Your baby is learning to take turns.

t44.text: Let your baby hold a spoon at meals. Mess is learning.

t45.text: Name the people in family photos with your baby.

t46.text: Give your baby time to try before you help.

t47.text: Mirror play is great fun. Point and say who is in the mirror.

t48.text: Short bursts of play are perfect. Babies tire quickly and that is fine.

t49.text: Clap and cheer for small tries. Your smile is the best reward.

t50.text: Copy your baby's sounds. It is a conversation.

t51.text: Bath time is play time: splash, pour and talk.

t52.text: Welcome. One small mission a week is enough to build a habit.

t53.text: Hard night? Today, a cuddle and a chat are enough.

t54.text: Get down to your child's eye level when you talk.

t55.text: Name feelings out loud: happy, sad, angry. It helps your child learn them.

t56.text: Offer help, then step back. Toddlers love to say "Me do it".

t57.text: Turn tidy-up into a game. Who can find the red blocks first?

t58.text: Read the same book again. Repetition builds words.

t59.text: Warn before changes: "2 more slides, then we go home."

t60.text: Let your child pick between 2 outfits. Small choices, big pride.

t61.text: Point at things on a walk and wait for your child to name them.

t62.text: Praise what you want to see more of.

t63.text: Outdoor play every day helps sleep, mood and muscles.

t64.text: Let your child help with simple cooking, like washing vegetables.

t65.text: Sing while you wait in a queue. It turns waiting into play.

t66.text: A hug can end a meltdown faster than words.

t67.text: Put a few toys away and swap them weekly. Old toys feel new again.

t68.text: Play hide and seek with a toy. Thinking and fun in one.

t69.text: Talk about what you are doing while you cook or clean.

t70.text: Stairs, slides and swings are all practice. The playground is a classroom.

t71.text: Not every day goes to plan. Tomorrow is a fresh start.

t72.text: Sometimes ask "How did you do that?" instead of only saying "Well done".

t73.text: Give your child a real job at home. Being needed feels good.

t74.text: Let your child explain the rules of a game to you.

t75.text: Count things together: stairs, apples, cars.

t76.text: Spot letters on signs when you are out.

t77.text: Make up a silly story together at bedtime.

t78.text: Let your child choose the book tonight.

t79.text: Talk about plans for tomorrow. It helps with time words.

t80.text: Draw together without a plan. See what appears.

t81.text: Ask your child to teach you something they learned.

t82.text: Rhyming games in the car make the trip shorter.

t83.text: Notice kindness out loud: "You shared your toy. That was kind."

t84.text: Board games teach waiting, taking turns and losing well.

t85.text: Leave time for free play. Boredom sparks ideas.

t86.text: Busy week? A 5-minute game still counts.

t87.text: You are doing better than you think.

t88.text: Small steps, every week. That is how skills grow.

t89.text: There is no perfect parent. Kind and present is enough.

t90.text: Take a photo of today's small win and tick it in Memories.

t92.text: Screens off for 5 minutes, eyes on each other. It all counts.

t93.text: Ask for help when you need it. Nobody can do it all alone.

t94.text: Every child learns some things fast and some things slowly. Both are normal.

t95.text: A calm voice helps a child stay calm.

t96.text: Write down a funny thing your child did this week.

t97.text: Play is how children learn. Your time together matters.

t98.text: Do this week's mission at a set time, like after breakfast.

t99.text: Low on energy? Pick the easiest way to practise and keep it short.

t100.text: Be as kind to yourself as you are to your child.

t101.text: Welcome to Hoppo. There is no homework in pregnancy. Read what helps and skip the rest.

t102.text: Your first week with Hoppo: pick 1 thing you are curious about and read just that. The rest can wait.

t103.text: Feeling heavy today? Put your feet up for 10 minutes. Nothing else needs to happen.

t104.text: Early pregnancy can be very tiring. Going to bed early is a sensible plan.

t105.text: A slow day is still a good day. Your body is doing a lot of work you cannot see.

t106.text: Let 1 job wait until tomorrow. The washing will still be there.

t107.text: Not sleeping well? A short rest in the afternoon can help, even if you do not fall asleep.

t108.text: Contact a midwife or doctor as soon as you know you are pregnant, so your care can start early.

t109.text: Ask your midwife which vitamins are recommended for you in pregnancy.

t110.text: Wash fruit, vegetables and salad well before you eat them.

t111.text: Feeling sick in the mornings? Eating something plain before you get up may help.

t112.text: Strong smells can make sickness worse. If you cannot keep food or drink down for 24 hours, contact your midwife or doctor.

t113.text: You decide when to share your news. There is no right week to tell people.

t114.text: Take a photo of your first scan picture, so you always have a copy.

t115.text: Keep a glass of water within reach. Drinking plenty of fluids can help with constipation.

t116.text: Before you take any medicine, ask a pharmacist, midwife or doctor if it is safe in pregnancy.

t117.text: Your bump may start to show in the middle months. Every bump grows at its own pace.

t118.text: Pelvic floor exercises are good to start in pregnancy. Ask your midwife to show you how.

t119.text: Keep up your normal daily activity if you feel well. Slow down when your body asks you to.

t120.text: Swimming and walking are gentle ways to stay active in pregnancy.

t121.text: Heartburn? Smaller meals more often can feel easier than 3 big ones.

t122.text: Feeling dizzy? Stand up slowly from a chair or bed.

t123.text: Wear flat, comfortable shoes as your bump grows. Your balance changes.

t124.text: Put a hand on your bump when your baby moves. Invite your partner or a friend to feel the kicks too.

t125.text: First movements may feel like flutters or bubbles. Every pregnancy is different.

t126.text: If your baby's movements slow down, stop or change, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away. Do not wait until the next day.

t127.text: Ask about antenatal classes near you. They are a good place to meet other parents-to-be.

t128.text: From 28 weeks, go to sleep on your side. If you wake up on your back, just turn onto your side.

t129.text: Mild itching can be common in pregnancy. Tell your midwife about any itching, especially on your hands and feet or worse at night.

t130.text: Feet up can ease swollen ankles at the end of the day. If your face, hands or feet swell suddenly, call your midwife or maternity unit straight away.

t131.text: Take a bump photo in the same spot each month. It makes a lovely series later.

t132.text: Write a short letter to your baby. Keep it in a box to read together one day.

t133.text: Start a small shelf of children's books before the birth. Ask family for a favourite from their own childhood.

t134.text: Wash a few first outfits for your baby ahead of time, so they are ready.

t135.text: Learn the signs that labour is starting. Ask your midwife what to look for and when to call.

t136.text: Write a simple birth plan with what matters to you. Share it with your midwife and birth partner.

t137.text: Plans can change on the day. A flexible birth plan leaves room for that.

t138.text: Try the route to the place of birth before the day. Think of a second way in case of traffic.

t139.text: Fit the baby car seat before the birth, and practise taking it in and out of the car.

t140.text: Ask your midwife about skin-to-skin contact after the birth. Think about what you would like.

t141.text: Ask your midwife about feeding your baby. Learning a little before the birth can help.

t142.text: Before the birth, set up a cot or Moses basket in your room. Your baby can sleep in the same room as you for the first 6 months.

t143.text: Buy nappies in 2 sizes, not just the smallest. Babies grow fast.

t144.text: Make a list of who to tell when your baby arrives. Someone else can send the news for you.

t145.text: Decide who will look after pets or older children when labour starts. Write their numbers down.

t146.text: Practise slow breathing for a few minutes a day. It can help you stay calm in labour.

t147.text: Needing the toilet at night is common late in pregnancy. A dim night light makes the trip safer and easier.

t148.text: Your due date is a guide. Many babies arrive in the weeks before or after it.

t149.text: In the last weeks, keep your pregnancy notes and a phone charger by the door.

t150.text: Read 1 Hoppo guide about labour together with your birth partner, so you both know what to expect.

t151.text: Agree who does what at home in the first weeks: meals, washing and visitors.

t152.text: Older children can help get ready. Let them pick a small toy for the new baby.

t153.text: Read a picture book about a new baby with an older child. It makes it easy to talk about the change.

t154.text: Grandparents may want to help. Tell them which kind of help you would like most.

t155.text: Talk with your partner or support person about what kind of parents you want to be. No answers needed yet.

t156.text: Moods can go up and down in pregnancy. Talk to your midwife if you often feel low or anxious.

t157.text: Ask for a seat on busy transport. People are often happy to help.

t158.text: Your birth partner can learn simple ways to help in labour, like a back rub or a cold drink.

t159.text: Plan a quiet day out with someone you love before your baby arrives.

t160.text: Hoppo's "Is this normal?" guides can help with small questions. For worries, call your midwife.

t161.text: Think about who you would like with you at the birth. You can change your mind later.

t162.text: Welcome to Hoppo. Look around at your own pace. There is nothing to catch up on.

t163.text: Today can be a rest day. Hoppo will still be here tomorrow.

t164.text: One hard day does not cancel all the good ones.

t165.text: Drink a glass of water and eat something before you look after everyone else.

t166.text: Step outside for 5 minutes, even in the rain. Fresh air helps big people and small people.

t167.text: Tick off a milestone in Hoppo when you notice it. Small moments are easy to forget.

t168.text: Send a friend a message today, just to say hello. Staying in touch helps on long days.

t169.text: Put a favourite photo where you see it every day. Small joys help on busy weeks.

t170.text: Your feelings matter too. Talk to someone you trust when things feel heavy.

t171.text: Write down 1 good thing about today before you sleep.

t172.text: Keep a list of 3 easy meals for busy days. On tired evenings, there is nothing to decide.

t173.text: Look at your logs once a week, not every hour. Patterns show over days.

t174.text: Share a Hoppo keepsake card with family far away. It helps them feel close.

t175.text: Put your phone in another room during a meal now and then. Quiet time is good for everyone.

t176.text: Put on music while you cook. It makes ordinary jobs feel lighter.

t177.text: If someone offers help, say yes and name 1 thing they can do.

t178.text: Stretch your back and shoulders for 2 minutes. Carrying and lifting add up.

t179.text: Notice what went well this week and do a little more of it.

t180.text: Every family does things its own way. What works for you is enough.

t181.text: In the first weeks, your baby sees best at about 20 to 30 cm. That is roughly the distance to your face during a feed.

t182.text: Newborns love the sound of your voice. Hum a slow tune during nappy changes.

t183.text: Tummy time can start from the first days, while your baby is awake and you are watching. A minute or 2 on your chest counts.

t184.text: Babies have a strong grip in the first weeks. Let your baby hold your finger and say hello.

t185.text: For every sleep, put your baby down on their back in their own cot or Moses basket. It is the safest way for babies to sleep.

t186.text: Use a firm, flat mattress with no pillows, bumpers or soft toys in the cot. A clear cot is a safe cot.

t187.text: Place your baby with their feet at the foot of the cot. This feet to foot position stops them wriggling down under the covers.

t188.text: For the first 6 months, keep your baby in the same room as you for every sleep, day and night.

t189.text: A room of 16 to 20°C is comfortable for baby sleep. Use light bedding and no hat, so your baby does not get too hot.

t190.text: Skin to skin cuddles are calming for many babies and parents. Try 10 minutes after a bath.

t191.text: Feed your baby when they show they are hungry, like rooting or sucking on their hands. Crying is often a late sign.

t192.text: Hello from Hoppo. Try logging a few feeds or naps this week. Patterns are easier to see when they are written down.

t193.text: Newborn sleep comes in short pieces. Sleep when you can, and let the housework wait.

t194.text: Soft black and white pictures can catch a young baby's eye. Hold one to the side and watch them look.

t195.text: Gently move your baby's legs in a cycling motion during a nappy change. Talk about what you are doing.

t196.text: Babies often have a fussy time in the evening. A walk around the room in your arms can help you both.

t197.text: A first smile often appears around 6 to 8 weeks. Smile back and give it a moment. Your baby is learning about faces.

t198.text: Carry your baby to the window and name what you see: tree, bird, car.

t199.text: Let visitors bring food or fold washing instead of only holding the baby.

t200.text: Gentle rocking, a low hum or a quiet room can all help a baby settle. Try 1 thing at a time.

t201.text: Watch for tired signs like yawning, staring away or rubbing eyes. Starting the wind-down early often helps.

t202.text: Around 3 months, many babies bring their hands together and look at them. Let them explore their fingers.

t203.text: Hang a toy just within reach while your baby lies on their back. Swiping at it is how reaching starts.

t204.text: Give your baby a rattle to hold. Shake it gently first and see if they try too.

t205.text: Babies often love a gentle game of peekaboo with a soft cloth from around 4 to 6 months.

t206.text: Lay your baby on their side with a toy in front, while you watch. It invites them to roll and reach.

t207.text: Speak to your baby in a slow, sing-song voice. Babies listen longer to this kind of playful talk.

t208.text: Place a toy a little in front of your baby during tummy time. It gives them a reason to lift and push.

t209.text: Let your baby feel different textures: a soft towel, a wooden spoon, a crinkly paper.

t210.text: Babies laugh at simple surprises. A gentle raspberry on the tummy is a classic.

t211.text: Sit your baby on your lap facing you and sing a song with actions. Help them clap or bounce along.

t212.text: Keep lights low and voices soft at night feeds. It helps your baby learn that night time is for sleeping.

t213.text: A regular bedtime routine like bath, feed, song and cot can help babies settle. Keep it short and the same.

t214.text: Record your baby's first giggle in Memories. You will want to hear it again.

t215.text: Around 6 months, many babies sit with a little support. Put cushions around them during floor play and stay close.

t216.text: Solid food usually starts at around 6 months. Breast milk or formula is still the main drink for the first year.

t217.text: Your baby may be ready for food when they can sit with a steady head, bring food to their mouth and swallow it.

t218.text: First foods can be simple. Soft cooked vegetables, mashed or as soft finger foods, are a good start.

t219.text: Offer the same vegetable a few times on different days. Babies often need many tries to get used to a new taste.

t220.text: Let your baby feed themselves with their hands at some meals. Picking up small soft pieces is great practice for fingers.

t221.text: Do not add salt or sugar to your baby's food. Let them taste food as it is.

t222.text: From around 6 months, offer sips of water from an open or free-flow cup with meals.

t223.text: Always stay with your baby when they eat. Sit them upright so they can see you and your plate.

t224.text: Eat together when you can. Babies learn a lot by watching you eat.

t225.text: Let your baby stop when they turn away or close their mouth. They are telling you they are full.

t226.text: Say the name of each food as your baby tries it. Mealtimes are word time too.

t227.text: Put a few toys in a basket and let your baby take them out. Then show how to put them back.

t228.text: Hide a toy under a cloth while your baby watches. Lifting the cloth is a big discovery.

t229.text: Babies love to drop things. Make it a game: they drop a ball, you say "Gone", and give it back.

t230.text: Bang 2 blocks together and pass one to your baby. Making noise is a skill too.

t231.text: Wave bye-bye every time someone leaves. Many babies start to copy it near their first birthday.

t232.text: Give your baby a plastic cup and spoon. Stirring and tapping like a grown-up is a favourite game near 1 year.

t233.text: Point at things and name them. Around the end of the first year, many babies start to point too.

t234.text: Crawling looks different for every baby. Some shuffle, some roll, some go straight to standing.

t235.text: Get down to crawling height and check the room for small objects and cables. Then let your baby explore.

t236.text: Sit on the floor with your legs open and roll a ball to your baby. Roll it back together.

t237.text: Let your baby pull up on a sturdy sofa while you stay near. Cruising along furniture often comes next.

t238.text: Show your baby a picture book with real photos. Name each thing and let them touch the page.

t239.text: At the end of each month, look back at your baby's milestones in Hoppo. It is easy to forget how far they have come.

t240.text: Welcome to Hoppo. The first year is busy, so the missions are short and simple.

t241.text: Nights are hard right now. Most babies start to sleep for longer stretches as they grow.

t242.text: Feeling worn out is common with a baby. Ask someone to take a walk with the pram so you can sleep.

t243.text: Practice did not go well? Your baby may simply be tired or hungry. Try again on a calmer day.

t244.text: Some days are just about getting through. You are still doing a good job.

t245.text: Add 1 word to what your child says. If they say "car", you say "blue car".

t246.text: Sing a song and stop before the last word. Let your child fill the gap.

t247.text: Talk about the pictures in a book, not only the words. Ask "Where is the cat?"

t248.text: When your child says a word wrong, say it back the right way. No need to correct.

t249.text: Make animal sounds together on a walk. A dog, a bird, a car all count as words.

t250.text: Put a favourite toy just out of reach. It gives your child a reason to ask.

t251.text: Talk on a toy phone together. Take turns saying hello and goodbye.

t252.text: Use real words for real things, like "spoon" and "jumper". Toddlers love grown-up words.

t253.text: Turn off background sound for a while. Quiet makes it easier to hear and copy words.

t254.text: Gestures are talking too. Pointing and waving show your child wants to share.

t255.text: A cardboard box can be a car, a house or a boat today. Simple toys spark big ideas.

t256.text: Build a tower and let your child knock it down. Then build it again together.

t257.text: Fill a bowl with a little water and give your child cups to pour. Stay right beside them and empty the bowl after.

t258.text: Play "Ready, steady, go" with a ball. Waiting for "go" is great practice.

t259.text: Make a simple puppet from a sock. Let it say hello at breakfast.

t260.text: Sort the washing together. Put all the socks in 1 pile and the shirts in another.

t261.text: Dance to 1 song together today. Fast, slow, then stop and freeze.

t262.text: Pretend play counts. Feed a teddy, put it to bed and say goodnight.

t263.text: Draw big circles and lines with chunky crayons. Scribbles are the first step to writing.

t264.text: Tantrums are common at this age. Your child is not being naughty. Big feelings are still new.

t265.text: Stay close and calm during a meltdown. You do not need to fix it, just be there.

t266.text: Say what you see: "You wanted the blue cup. You are cross." Feeling heard helps.

t267.text: Hunger and tiredness make feelings bigger. A snack or a rest can prevent a storm.

t268.text: After a tantrum, move on to something new together. There is no need for a long talk.

t269.text: Say what to do, not only what not to do: "Feet on the floor" instead of "No climbing".

t270.text: Take 3 slow breaths before you answer a meltdown. Calm is catching.

t271.text: Read a book about feelings together. Point to the faces and name them.

t272.text: Make a picture chart of the bedtime steps. Your toddler can point to what comes next.

t273.text: Make the last hour before bed calm and quiet. Dim lights help the body get ready.

t274.text: A favourite soft toy can make bedtime feel safer for a toddler.

t275.text: Note bedtimes in the Hoppo sleep log for a week. You may spot the time your child falls asleep most easily.

t276.text: Let your toddler say goodnight to a few toys or rooms. A small goodbye ritual helps them let go of the day.

t277.text: Offer a new food next to a food your child already likes. No pressure to try it.

t278.text: Let your toddler touch, smell or lick a new food without eating it. Every small step counts as trying.

t279.text: Put a little of the family meal on your toddler's plate. Eating the same food as you feels grown-up.

t280.text: Give your toddler a small job at mealtimes, like setting out spoons. Helpers often eat with more interest.

t281.text: Cut grapes and cherry tomatoes into quarters lengthways for children under 5. Small round foods are a choking risk.

t282.text: Let your child serve themselves with a small spoon. Some spills are part of learning.

t283.text: Toddler appetites change from day to day. Trust them to eat what they need.

t284.text: There is no perfect age for potty learning. Many families start around 2 to 2 and a half, when their child shows signs of being ready.

t285.text: Let your child sit on the potty with clothes on first. Getting used to it is the first step.

t286.text: Accidents are part of potty learning. Clean up calmly and say "Next time".

t287.text: Read a book about the potty together. It makes the idea familiar and fun.

t288.text: Say a short, warm goodbye at daycare. Then go. A long goodbye can make it harder.

t289.text: Tell your child who will pick them up today. Knowing the plan helps them feel safe.

t290.text: Ask the daycare team what made your child laugh today. It gives you something to talk about.

t291.text: A small thing from home, like a photo, can help your child settle at daycare.

t292.text: Tears at drop-off often stop soon after you leave. Ask the team how the day went.

t293.text: Give each child a little time alone with you this week, even 10 minutes.

t294.text: Let your toddler help with a baby sibling: fetch a nappy or sing a song.

t295.text: Notice when siblings play nicely and say it out loud.

t296.text: Use a timer for taking turns with a favourite toy. The timer decides, not you.

t297.text: Jump in puddles with good boots on. Wet weather is play weather too.

t298.text: Collect leaves, stones or sticks on a walk. Sort them by size at home.

t299.text: Let your child walk part of the way instead of riding. Slow walks are full of things to see.

t300.text: Blow bubbles outside and let your child chase them. Running, reaching and laughing all at once.

t301.text: Add your child's new words to a log this month. You will be surprised how fast the list grows.

t302.text: Hard day of tantrums? You stayed. That is what your child will remember.

t303.text: Mission did not work yesterday? Toddlers have off days too. Try again another time.

t304.text: Short on sleep? Pick 1 quiet game today, like reading on the sofa.

t305.text: Not every mission ends well. A laugh together still counts as a good session.

t306.text: Feeling worn out? A walk to the window to wave at cars is enough for today.

t307.text: Welcome. Toddlers learn best in short bursts. 5 minutes a day is plenty.

t308.text: Welcome. Check the milestones in Hoppo to see what your child may enjoy next.

t309.text: Ask open questions like "What happened next?" They invite longer answers than yes or no.

t310.text: When your child tells a long story, listen to the end. Then ask 1 question about it.

t311.text: Use new words in everyday talk, like "enormous" or "curious". Children pick them up fast.

t312.text: Wonder out loud together: "Why do you think the leaves fall?" No right answer needed.

t313.text: Talk in the car or on the bus. Side by side, children often share more.

t314.text: Play "Tell me how": ask your child to explain how to brush teeth, step by step.

t315.text: Ask your child to retell a favourite story in their own words. Then swap roles.

t316.text: Stop before the last page and ask how the story might end.

t317.text: Let your child "read" a familiar book to you from memory. It is real reading practice.

t318.text: Run your finger under the words as you read. Your child sees that print has meaning.

t319.text: Write your child's name on their drawings together. Their own letters come first.

t320.text: Play "I spy" with first sounds: "I spy something that starts with mmm."

t321.text: Keep books in a low basket where your child can reach them any time.

t322.text: Set the table together and count: 1 plate, 2 plates, 3 plates for 3 people.

t323.text: Line up toys from smallest to biggest. Putting things in order is early maths.

t324.text: Ask "Who has more?" when you share out a snack. Comparing is a number game.

t325.text: Cut a sandwich into halves and quarters. Fractions can be tasty.

t326.text: Look for shapes on a walk: round wheels, square windows, triangle roofs.

t327.text: Bake together and let your child pour and measure. Cups and spoons are maths tools.

t328.text: Numbers and letters are for play at this age. If interest fades, try again another day.

t329.text: Invite 1 friend over for an hour. Small playdates are easier than big groups.

t330.text: Play shop or kitchen with a friend. Pretend play builds social skills.

t331.text: If your child grabs a toy, say what the other child feels: "Sam looks sad."

t332.text: Practise asking to join in: "Can I play too?" Act it out with toys first.

t333.text: Friendships come and go at this age. Changing best friends every week is normal.

t334.text: Help your child find words for a problem: "Can I have a turn when you finish?"

t335.text: Make a feelings face game. Take turns showing happy, worried or surprised.

t336.text: After a big feeling passes, talk about it calmly. "You were very cross. What helped?"

t337.text: All feelings are allowed. Hitting is not. Say both, calmly.

t338.text: Breathe together like blowing out birthday candles. It helps a body calm down.

t339.text: Read a story and ask how a character feels. Stories make feelings easier to talk about.

t340.text: Let your child dress themselves, even if the jumper is back to front.

t341.text: Put a small step by the sink so your child can wash their hands alone.

t342.text: Give your child a small bag to carry their own things on outings.

t343.text: Let your child make their own simple snack, like spreading butter on bread.

t344.text: Practise shoes, coat and zip on calm mornings, not when you are in a hurry.

t345.text: Practise short times apart before kindergarten starts, like an hour with a grandparent or friend.

t346.text: Ask about kindergarten with a game: "Tell me 1 thing you ate and 1 thing you played."

t347.text: Read a picture book about starting kindergarten in the weeks before the first day.

t348.text: Visit the kindergarten together before the first day if you can. Familiar feels safer.

t349.text: WHO advises at least 3 hours of active play a day for children aged 3 to 4, spread across the day. Any movement counts.

t350.text: Build a den from sticks in the park or blankets at home. Big ideas need big spaces.

t351.text: Take the same walk in each season. Ask your child what has changed since last time.

t352.text: Draw a chalk path on the ground: hop, jump, then walk like a crab.

t353.text: Watch a bug together and describe it. Small things outside spark big questions.

t354.text: WHO advises no more than 1 hour of screen time a day for children aged 2 to 4. Less is better.

t355.text: Watch together when you can and talk about what you see. Screens can be shared too.

t356.text: Keep screens out of the hour before bed. A story or a cuddle helps sleep come.

t357.text: Practise sitting for a short story or game. Listening for 5 minutes is a school skill.

t358.text: Let your child practise opening their lunch box and bottle on their own.

t359.text: Play "Simon says". Following simple instructions is great school practice.

t360.text: Welcome. Small games each week help your child grow in talking, play and confidence.

t361.text: Pick 1 skill in Learn this week that your child already enjoys. An easy start.

t362.text: A grumpy day is not a step back. Big feelings use a lot of energy.

t363.text: Did practice not work today? Read a book together instead. That counts too.

t364.text: Rushed morning? Tomorrow can be calmer. Today is already enough.

t365.text: Tired after kindergarten? Skip the mission and play what your child wants.
