crying.title: My baby cries a lot
crying.intro: All babies cry, and some cry much more than others. Long crying spells in a healthy baby are often called colic.
common: Colic means a healthy baby cries for more than 3 hours a day, on 3 or more days a week, for at least 1 week.
It usually starts when a baby is a few weeks old and stops by 3 to 4 months.
Crying is often worse in the late afternoon and evening.
During a spell, babies may go red, clench their fists, pull up their knees or arch their back.
Hunger, a dirty nappy, trapped wind and tiredness are common reasons for crying too.
helps: Hold and cuddle your baby, and rock them gently over your shoulder or in a pram.
Keep your baby upright during feeds, and burp them after feeds.
A warm bath or calm background noise can help some babies settle.
Keep feeding as usual. Breastfeeding mothers do not need to change their diet for colic.
If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby down safely in the cot, leave the room for a few minutes and breathe. Ask someone to take over if you can.
Never shake a baby. It can cause serious brain injury.
Ask your doctor before trying colic drops, or herbal or homeopathic remedies. Most have no proven benefit.
help: You are worried about the crying, or nothing seems to help.
You find it hard to cope.
Your baby is not gaining weight as expected.
Long crying spells continue after 4 months.
Your baby seems pale, or keeps vomiting.
urgent: You feel you might hurt your baby. Put your baby down safely in their cot and get help now.
The cry is weak, high-pitched or does not sound like your baby's normal cry.
Your baby has other worrying signs, such as a high temperature, floppiness or trouble breathing.

spitting_up.title: My baby spits up milk
spitting_up.intro: Bringing up a little milk during or after a feed is very common. It is called reflux and usually gets better on its own.
common: Reflux usually starts before 8 weeks and improves by about 1 year.
A happy baby who brings up a little milk and is gaining weight usually does not need to see a doctor.
It happens because the ring of muscle at the top of the stomach is still weak. It gets stronger as your baby grows.
helps: Hold your baby upright during feeds and for 10 to 15 minutes afterwards.
Burp your baby regularly during feeds.
Ask your health visitor or midwife to check your feeding position or bottle technique.
Always lay your baby down to sleep flat on their back. Do not raise the head end of the cot.
help: Things do not improve after trying these ideas.
Reflux starts for the first time after 6 months, or continues after 1 year.
Your baby is not gaining weight, or is losing weight.
urgent: Their vomit is green or yellow, or has blood in it.
Your baby vomits forcefully, or cannot keep any fluids down.
There is blood in their poo, or their tummy is swollen or tender.
Your baby refuses to feed, cries and cannot be comforted, or has a high temperature.

safe_sleep.title: How should my baby sleep safely?
safe_sleep.intro: A few simple habits lower the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). They matter most in the first 6 months and apply for the whole first year.
common: Babies sleep safest on their back, in their own cot or Moses basket, in your room.
Once babies can roll both ways on their own, you do not need to turn them back.
A room temperature of about 16 to 20°C is comfortable for most babies.
helps: Put your baby on their back for every sleep, with their feet at the foot of the cot.
Keep the cot in your room for at least the first 6 months, day and night.
Use a firm, flat mattress. Keep the cot clear: no pillows, duvets, bumpers, soft toys, pods or nests.
Use light bedding or a baby sleeping bag. Feel their chest or the back of their neck to check they are not too hot.
Take off hats and extra layers when you come indoors or get into the car.
Keep the home and car smoke-free.
A dummy at sleep times can lower the risk. If you breastfeed, wait until feeding is going well before you offer one.
If you swaddle, always lay your baby on their back, keep the wrap loose at the hips, and stop when your baby starts trying to roll.
Do not use sleep positioners, inclined sleepers, weighted blankets or weighted sleeping bags.
Never fall asleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.
Do not share a bed if your baby was born early or small, or if anyone in the bed smokes, has drunk alcohol, used drugs or taken medicine that makes them drowsy.
Do not leave your baby sleeping in a car seat for long after a journey.
help: You have questions about slings, swaddling or bed sharing.
You are worried about how your baby sleeps or breathes.
urgent: Your baby is hard to wake, floppy, very pale or blue, or has trouble breathing. Call your emergency number.

baby_sleep.title: My baby wakes up a lot at night
baby_sleep.intro: Night waking is normal for babies. Sleep changes a lot in the first year, and every baby is different.
common: Newborns sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day in short stretches and wake to feed.
From 3 to 6 months, some babies sleep 5 hours or more at night. Many do not, and that is normal too.
From 4 to 11 months, most babies sleep about 12 to 16 hours a day, including naps.
Growth spurts, teething and illness can change sleep for a while.
helps: Show your baby the difference between day and night: daylight and play in the day, low light and quiet voices at night.
Start a short, calm bedtime routine, such as a bath, pyjamas, a story and a cuddle.
Rest when your baby sleeps, and share night duties when you can.
Log sleep in Care, Sleep. It helps you see the pattern over a week.
help: You are exhausted and finding it hard to cope.
You would like help building a routine.
Your baby seems unwell, or sleep changes suddenly with other symptoms.

teething.title: Is my baby teething?
teething.intro: Most babies get their first tooth around 6 months, but anything from before 4 months to after 12 months can be normal.
common: Sore, red gums, dribbling, chewing on things, one flushed cheek and poorer sleep are common.
Teething does not cause a fever. A temperature of 38°C or higher has another cause.
The front teeth usually come first, around 6 months, and most children have all their milk teeth by 2 to 3 years.
Some teeth come through with no fuss at all.
helps: Give your baby a clean, cool teething ring or a firm toy to chew on.
Gently rub their gums with a clean finger.
Wipe away dribble often to protect the skin on their chin.
Start brushing as soon as the first tooth appears.
Avoid teething necklaces, numbing gels and homeopathic teething products. Necklaces can cause choking or strangling.
Tick each new tooth in Memories, Teeth.
help: Your baby seems unwell, or you are worried about any symptom.
Your baby has diarrhoea. There is no good evidence that teething causes it, so look for another cause.
urgent: Your baby has a temperature of 38°C or higher and is under 3 months. See the guide on high temperature.

first_foods.title: When does my baby start solid food?
first_foods.intro: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends starting solid food at around 6 months. Some European health services, including the one in Slovenia, say between 4 and 6 months, but never before 17 weeks. Ask your paediatrician or health visitor what is right for your baby.
common: A baby is ready when 3 signs appear together: they can sit with their head steady, pick up food and put it in their mouth, and swallow food instead of pushing it back out.
Chewing fists, waking at night or wanting more milk are normal and do not mean your baby is ready.
Gagging is common while babies learn to eat. Watery eyes and pushing food out are part of learning.
A new food can take 10 tries or more before your baby accepts it.
helps: Start with a few spoonfuls or soft pieces of single vegetables or fruit, such as broccoli, carrot, apple or pear.
Offer finger food about the size of your finger, soft enough to squash.
Give sips of water from an open cup with meals.
Introduce common allergens, such as egg, peanut, gluten and fish, one at a time in small amounts.
Always stay with your baby while they eat.
Do not add salt or sugar. No honey before 1 year, and no cow's milk as the main drink before 1 year.
Avoid whole nuts, hard raw foods and whole grapes or cherry tomatoes. Cut small round foods lengthways into quarters.
help: Your baby was born early. Ask when to start.
Your baby has a reaction to a food, such as a rash.
urgent: Your baby is choking and cannot cough, cry or breathe. Call your emergency number and start first aid.
Swelling of the lips or face, or trouble breathing, after a new food. Call your emergency number.

fever.title: My child has a high temperature
fever.intro: A temperature of 38°C or higher counts as a fever. It is very common in young children and is usually the body fighting an infection.
common: Most fevers pass within 1 to 4 days.
Your child may feel hot, look flushed, be sweaty or be more tired and clingy than usual.
A digital thermometer under the arm is the simplest way to check.
helps: Offer plenty of fluids. Keep breastfeeding if you breastfeed.
Keep your child at home to rest, and check on them regularly, including at night.
Dress your child in light clothes. Do not wrap them up warmly, and do not sponge them with cold water.
Only give fever medicine as the pack or a pharmacist says. Never give aspirin to children.
help: Your baby is 3 to 6 months with a temperature of 39°C or higher.
The fever lasts more than 2 days, or more than 1 day in a child under 2.
The temperature keeps going above 40°C.
Your child has a rash, is not eating, or is not their usual self.
Your child shows signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth or no tears.
urgent: Your baby is under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher.
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it.
A stiff neck, or your child is bothered by light.
A fit (seizure), if it is the first one.
Very cold hands and feet, or blue, grey or very pale skin or lips.
Your child is hard to wake, very confused or very agitated.
Trouble breathing or very fast breathing.

tantrums.title: My toddler has tantrums
tantrums.intro: Tantrums are a normal part of growing up. They usually start around 18 months and become much less common by 4 years.
common: Toddlers have big feelings and few words to express them, so frustration comes out as a tantrum.
Tiredness, hunger, jealousy and wanting attention are common triggers.
Hitting, biting and pushing are also common at this age and do not mean your child will be aggressive later.
Tantrums get less frequent as talking improves.
helps: Check the basics first: is your child hungry or tired?
Distract your child early, before the tantrum builds.
Stay calm. Shouting back makes the tantrum last longer. Ignore people watching.
Stick to your decision. Giving in teaches that tantrums work.
Name the feeling: "You are angry because we left the park."
Praise calm moments and give lots of affection.
help: You are seriously worried about your child's behaviour.
Tantrums are very frequent or very long, or your child often hurts themselves or others.
You feel you are losing your temper often and need support.

picky_eating.title: My toddler is a picky eater
picky_eating.intro: It is perfectly normal for toddlers to refuse new foods or eat very little at some meals.
common: Appetite changes from day to day. Look at what your child eats over a week, not one meal.
A child who is active, growing and well is usually getting enough.
Some foods need many tries before a child accepts them, and tastes change over time.
helps: Eat together and eat the same food. Children learn by copying.
Offer small portions and praise any eating, even a little.
If food is refused, take it away calmly and offer it again another day.
Limit snacks to about 2 healthy ones a day, so your child is hungry at meals.
Try the same food in a new way, such as raw grated carrot instead of cooked.
Do not force eating, and do not use sweets as a reward.
help: Your child is not growing or gaining weight, or seems unwell.
Your child eats only a very small number of foods.
Meal times are causing a lot of worry for you.

talking.title: My child is not talking much yet
talking.intro: Children learn to talk at different ages. Everyday chat is the best practice there is.
common: Around 15 months, many children try 1 or 2 words other than mama or dada.
Around 18 months, many try 3 or more words and follow simple requests.
Around 2 years, many put 2 words together, like "more milk".
Children often understand much more than they can say.
Children who hear 2 languages at home learn both. Keep using your home languages.
helps: Name things as you do everyday jobs: getting dressed, cooking, shopping.
Watch where your child looks and talk about what they see.
Give simple choices: "Apple or banana?"
Read picture books and sing songs with actions.
Wait a few seconds after you ask something, so your child has time to answer.
Avoid screens for children under 2. When you do use them, watch together and talk about what you see.
help: By about 12 months, your child does not use sounds or gestures to ask for things, or does not play games like peekaboo.
Your child has no words by about 18 months, or does not point or wave.
Your child does not put 2 words together by about 2 years.
Your child does not seem to understand simple words or requests.
Your child loses words or skills they had before.
You are worried about your child's hearing. A hearing check is quick and easy to arrange.

potty.title: When is my child ready for the potty?
potty.intro: Most children are ready to start between 18 months and 3 years, often around 2. Every child is different, and there is no need to rush.
common: Accidents are normal and part of learning.
Some children tell you when they need to go, and some do not. Both are normal.
Signs of readiness include staying dry for 2 hours, knowing when they wee or poo, disliking a wet nappy and following simple requests. Not all signs need to be there.
Being dry at night usually comes months or even years after being dry in the day. Bedwetting is common even at school age.
helps: Get your child used to the potty first with books, a doll or sitting practice.
Pick a calm time to start, not during a move or the arrival of a new baby.
Switch to pants in the day. Keep nappies for naps and nights for now.
Offer the potty after waking, after meals, before going out and before sleep. If nothing happens after 3 to 5 minutes, let your child get up.
Praise the effort, not just the result. Clean up accidents calmly.
Choose clothes that are easy to pull down.
help: Your child is constipated: hard, pebble-like poos or straining. Treat this before stopping nappies.
Progress is very slow, or your child is still in nappies when school is getting close.
Your child was dry but has started wetting often again.

screens.title: How much screen time is OK?
screens.intro: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends sitting less and playing more for children under 5.
common: Under 2 years: screen time is not recommended, except video calls with family.
At 2 years: no more than 1 hour a day. Less is better.
From 3 to 4 years: no more than 1 hour a day.
From 1 to 4 years, children need at least 3 hours of active play spread over the day.
helps: Watch together and talk about what you see.
Keep screens out of meals and the hour before bed.
Swap some screen time for books, songs and play.
Avoid keeping children strapped in a pram or seat for more than 1 hour at a time.
help: Screens are causing a lot of conflict at home.
You are worried about your child's sleep, speech or play.

low_mood.title: I have felt low since my baby was born
low_mood.intro: Feeling tearful, anxious or irritable in the first days after birth is very common. It is called the baby blues and usually passes within 2 weeks.
common: Postnatal depression is common and treatable. It can start in pregnancy or any time in the first year.
Signs include low mood, not enjoying things, feeling unable to cope, guilt, constant worry, poor sleep even when you can rest, and trouble bonding with your baby.
Partners and fathers can get depressed after a birth too.
helps: Talk to someone you trust about how you feel.
Accept practical help with meals, chores or night feeds. A partner can take a night feed so you can sleep.
Rest when you can, and get outside for a short walk.
Join a parent and baby group. Many parents feel the same.
Avoid using alcohol to cope.
help: The low feelings last more than 2 weeks or get worse.
You find it hard to cope day to day.
You have only some of the signs. Help works, and the earlier, the better.
urgent: You have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Get help now: call your emergency number or a crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency department.

morning_sickness.title: I feel sick all the time
morning_sickness.intro: Feeling sick or being sick is very common in early pregnancy. It can happen at any time of the day, not only in the morning.
common: It usually starts in the first weeks, is often worst between weeks 6 and 12, and eases by weeks 14 to 20.
It does not harm your baby.
It is more common in a first pregnancy, with twins, or if you get travel sickness or migraines.
helps: Rest when you can. Tiredness makes nausea worse.
Eat small, plain, starchy snacks often, such as crackers or toast.
Try cold food if the smell of hot food bothers you.
Sip drinks little and often through the day.
Ask a pharmacist before trying ginger supplements or other remedies.
help: Changes to food and rest are not enough. Treatment is available.
You also have tummy pain, a high temperature or pain when you pee.
urgent: You cannot keep any food or drink down for 24 hours.
Your pee is very dark, or you have not peed for more than 8 hours.
You feel very weak, dizzy or faint when you stand up.
You vomit blood.

preg_sleep.title: I am so tired and cannot sleep
preg_sleep.intro: Tiredness is very common, especially in the first 12 weeks and again near the end. Sleep often gets harder as the bump grows.
common: Hormones make many people very tired in early pregnancy.
Later, the bump, needing to pee and leg cramps can wake you up.
Vivid dreams about the baby or the birth are common.
helps: Go to sleep on your side, left or right. From 28 weeks, sleeping on your back is linked to a higher risk for your baby.
If you wake on your back, simply turn onto your side.
A pillow under your bump or between your knees can help.
Avoid long naps late in the day, and cut caffeine in the evening.
Stay active in the day, for example with a walk or a swim.
Accept offers of help, and rest with your feet up.
help: Lack of sleep is making you feel low.
You also feel hopeless or have lost interest in things you usually enjoy. This can be a sign of depression, and help is available.

movements.title: My baby is moving less
movements.intro: Getting to know your baby's movements is one of the most important things you can do in pregnancy.
common: Most people first feel movements between 16 and 24 weeks, often later in a first pregnancy.
Early movements feel like fluttering or swirling. Later you feel kicks and jerks.
There is no set number of kicks. What matters is your own baby's usual pattern.
Babies keep moving right up to and during labour.
helps: Notice when your baby is usually active, for example in the evening.
Do not rely on a home heartbeat monitor. Hearing a heartbeat does not mean your baby is well.
Tell your midwife if you have not felt any movement by 24 weeks.
help: You are unsure whether the pattern has changed. It is always fine to call.
urgent: Your baby is moving less than usual, or the usual pattern has changed. Call your midwife or maternity unit straight away, even at night. Do not wait until the next day.
You cannot feel your baby moving. Call your midwife or maternity unit straight away.

hospital_bag.title: What do I pack for the birth?
hospital_bag.intro: Pack your bag at least 3 weeks before your due date. Only a few babies arrive on the due date itself.
common: Most people pack one bag for themselves and one for the baby.
You need a car seat to drive your baby home, so fit it before the birth.
helps: For you: pregnancy notes and birth plan, loose clothes, a dressing gown and slippers, and nightwear that opens at the front if you plan to breastfeed.
Also for you: 2 packs of maternity pads, comfortable underwear, 2 or 3 comfortable bras and breast pads, a wash bag, lip balm and your regular medicines.
Snacks, drinks, a water bottle, a phone charger with a long cable, and something to pass the time.
For your baby: vests, sleepsuits, a hat, socks, an outfit for going home, nappies, wipes or cotton wool, muslins and a blanket.
Keep the maternity unit number and your hospital reference in your phone and on paper.
help: You are not sure what your hospital provides. This differs between places.

labour_signs.title: Is this labour?
labour_signs.intro: Labour can start slowly. The early part can last hours or even days, and many people stay at home for it.
common: Signs include regular tightenings, a show (a pink, jelly-like plug of mucus), backache, an urge to go to the toilet, and your waters breaking.
Practice contractions (Braxton Hicks) are usually painless and irregular.
Real contractions get longer, stronger and closer together.
helps: Keep moving, eat and drink, and use the breathing exercises you learned.
A warm bath or a back massage from your birth partner can help.
Time the contractions: how long they last and how far apart they are.
Call your midwife or maternity unit when contractions are regular, or if you are unsure.
help: Your waters break. Use a pad, not a tampon, so the fluid can be checked.
You are worried about anything at all.
urgent: You have bleeding.
Your baby is moving less than usual.
You are under 37 weeks and think labour has started.
A contraction lasts longer than 2 minutes, or you have 6 or more in 10 minutes.
Your waters are green or brown, or smell bad.
You feel a strong urge to push and think the baby is coming now. Call your emergency number.

crawling.title: My baby is not crawling yet
crawling.intro: Babies start to move around at very different ages, and some never crawl on hands and knees at all.
common: In a large World Health Organization (WHO) study, healthy babies started crawling on hands and knees anywhere from about 5 to 13 and a half months.
About 4 in 100 babies in that study never crawled on hands and knees.
Some babies bottom-shuffle, roll or slide on their tummy instead. These all count as getting around.
helps: Give your baby plenty of floor time on a safe, clean surface.
Put toys just out of reach to encourage your baby to move.
Keep time in seats, bouncers and carriers short.
Try the Crawl to a toy mission in Learn.
help: Your baby does not sit without support by about 9 months.
Your baby does not try to move around by about 12 months.
Your baby uses one side of their body much more than the other.
Your baby loses skills they had before.

colds.title: My baby has a cold
colds.intro: Young children catch many colds, especially in their first years of daycare. Most get better on their own.
common: A runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a cough and a slightly raised temperature are common.
In babies, a cold can turn into bronchiolitis, with a cough, faster breathing and trouble feeding. It is usually worst on days 3 to 5.
A cough can last up to 3 weeks.
helps: Offer smaller feeds more often, and extra drinks for older children.
Keep your baby upright when awake to make breathing easier.
Check on your child regularly, including at night.
Keep the home smoke-free.
Saline drops can help a blocked nose. Do not use medicated nose drops or cold medicines without asking a doctor.
Wash hands often and keep newborns away from people with colds.
help: The cold is getting worse, or your child is not their usual self.
Your baby feeds or drinks much less than usual.
There has been no wet nappy for 12 hours or more.
Your child is over 3 months with a temperature of 39°C or higher.
urgent: Your baby is under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher.
Your child struggles to breathe, grunts, wheezes, has flaring nostrils, or the skin pulls in under the ribs.
Pauses in breathing.
Blue or grey skin, lips or tongue.
Your child is floppy or cannot stay awake.

nappy_rash.title: My baby has nappy rash
nappy_rash.intro: Nappy rash is common and can usually be treated at home.
common: Red or sore patches on the bottom or in the nappy area. Spots and dry skin can appear too.
It is caused by wee and poo on the skin, rubbing, and sometimes by soaps or scented wipes.
It is more likely with diarrhoea or after antibiotics.
helps: Change wet or dirty nappies as soon as you can.
Clean with water or fragrance-free wipes, and pat dry instead of rubbing.
Leave the nappy off for a while each day.
Make sure nappies fit well and are not too tight.
Use a thick layer of plain barrier cream, such as zinc cream, at each change. A pharmacist can advise.
Avoid soap, bubble bath, lotions and talc in the nappy area.
help: The rash is not better after about a week, or it gets worse or spreads.
Blisters, crusts or pus-filled spots appear.
Your baby seems very uncomfortable.
Your baby has a high temperature.
urgent: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it.

constipation.title: My child is constipated
constipation.intro: Constipation is common in babies and young children, especially when starting solid food or potty training.
common: Fewer than 3 poos a week, large hard poos, or small pellets.
Straining, pain when pooing, or a tummy ache that eases after a poo.
Older children may have runny poo leaking around hard poo.
helps: Offer plenty of drinks. Formula-fed babies can have extra water between feeds.
Offer fruit and vegetables at meals once your baby eats solid food.
Encourage active play every day.
Sit your child on the potty after meals, with their feet flat, and praise them for trying.
Stay calm about it. Pressure can make it worse.
help: You think your child is constipated. Early help makes it easier to treat.
Your baby is under 1 year and seems constipated.
There is blood in their poo.
Your child is in pain, or is not eating well.
urgent: A swollen tummy with vomiting, or vomit that is green.
Your baby is under 1 and very unwell.

teeth_care.title: How do I look after my baby's teeth?
teeth_care.intro: Start brushing as soon as the first tooth appears. Good habits early protect the milk teeth.
common: Brush at least twice a day, once just before bed.
Use fluoride toothpaste: a smear the size of a grain of rice for babies and toddlers, and a pea-sized amount from about 2 to 3 years. Ask your dentist which amount is advised where you live.
Children need an adult to help or check their brushing until at least age 7.
helps: Brush in small circles over every tooth.
Let your child spit out the toothpaste, but do not rinse their mouth with water.
Bottles are for milk or water only, never juice or sweet drinks.
From 6 months, offer drinks in an open or free-flowing cup.
Keep sweet foods and drinks to meal times.
Take your child along to your own dental check-ups so they get used to the dentist.
help: You see white or brown spots on the teeth.
Your child has tooth pain or swollen gums.
You want to find a dentist for your child.
urgent: A knocked-out or broken tooth after a fall. Contact a dentist the same day.

head_bump.title: My child bumped their head
head_bump.intro: Small bumps on the head are very common in toddlers and usually not serious.
common: A lump or bruise on the head is common after a fall.
A mild headache, feeling sick, tiredness or being more irritable can last a few days.
Most children recover fully.
helps: Hold something cold wrapped in a cloth on the bump.
Stay with your child for the first 48 hours and watch how they behave.
Keep them calm and away from climbing or cycling for 48 hours.
Contact your doctor if your child does not seem quite right in the days after.
help: Symptoms last longer than 2 weeks.
Your child does not seem quite themselves.
urgent: Your baby is under 1, or there is a large swelling on the head.
Your child was knocked out, even briefly, or is hard to wake.
Vomiting after the injury, or a headache that does not ease.
A fit, or problems with seeing, walking, balance or speaking.
Neck pain, double vision, or weakness or numbness in the arms or legs.
Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears.
A fall from a height, or a change in behaviour, especially in a child under 5.

foods_avoid.title: What should I not eat in pregnancy?
foods_avoid.intro: Most foods are fine in pregnancy. A few carry a small risk of infection or contain things that can harm your baby, so it is best to avoid or limit them.
common: Avoid unpasteurised milk. Avoid soft cheeses with a white rind, such as brie and camembert, and soft blue cheeses, unless they are cooked until steaming hot.
Avoid raw or undercooked meat, liver and liver products, and cold cured meats such as salami unless cooked.
Avoid raw or smoked fish and shellfish, unless cooked. Avoid shark, swordfish and marlin.
Avoid pâté, ready-made deli salads, raw sprouts and unpasteurised juice.
Cook eggs until the white and yolk are solid, unless your local health service says eggs with a safety mark are fine to eat runny.
Do not drink alcohol. No amount is known to be safe in pregnancy.
helps: Hard cheeses made from pasteurised milk are fine. Health services differ on pasteurised soft cheese, so the safest choice is to eat it cooked.
Eat well-cooked meat and fish, and sushi made with cooked fish.
Limit tuna and oily fish such as salmon and mackerel to about 2 portions a week.
Limit caffeine to about 2 mugs of instant coffee a day. Tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate count too.
Keep herbal tea to about 4 cups a day.
Wash fruit, vegetables and salad well.
Let someone else clean the cat litter, and wear gloves for gardening. This lowers the risk of toxoplasmosis.
help: You ate something on the list and feel unwell. A small amount usually causes no harm if you feel well.
You have diarrhoea or vomiting that lasts more than 2 days.
You want advice on vitamins or supplements.

preg_exercise.title: Can I exercise while pregnant?
preg_exercise.intro: Staying active is good for you and your baby. The aim is about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, in short sessions if you like.
common: Moderate means you can still talk, but not sing.
Walking, swimming, cycling on an exercise bike and pregnancy yoga are good choices.
If you were active before, you can usually continue, with care.
helps: If you are new to exercise, start with about 10 minutes a day and build up slowly.
Do muscle-strengthening activities twice a week, such as yoga or carrying shopping.
Drink water, keep cool and eat something before you start.
Tell your trainer or instructor that you are pregnant.
Switch to gentler activity later in pregnancy if it feels better.
Avoid starting a new hard sport, contact sports, sports with a risk of falling, and scuba diving.
Avoid lying flat on your back for long in later pregnancy.
Avoid saunas, hot yoga and exercise in the heat of the day.
help: You have a health condition. Ask which activities are safe for you.
You were not active before and are not sure where to start.
urgent: You have bleeding, fluid leaking, regular painful contractions, or a change in your baby's movements. Stop and get help.
You have chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, dizziness, headache or blurred vision, sudden swelling, or pain or swelling in the calf. Stop exercising.

enough_milk.title: Is my baby getting enough milk?
enough_milk.intro: Many parents worry about this, especially in the first weeks of breastfeeding. Nappies and weight are the best guide.
common: Babies lose a little weight in the first days, then gain steadily.
In the first 2 days, 2 or 3 wet nappies a day is usual.
From about day 5, expect at least 6 heavy wet nappies a day.
From about day 4, breastfed babies usually have at least 2 soft yellow poos a day in the first weeks.
Newborns feed often, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours.
helps: Feed as often and for as long as your baby wants.
Watch for early hunger signs such as stirring, rooting and sucking their hands, before crying starts.
Offer both breasts and swap the side you start with.
Listen for swallowing during the feed.
Log feeds and nappies in Care if it helps you see the pattern.
help: You are worried about how much milk your baby gets. Ask for help early.
Feeding hurts, or your baby struggles to latch.
Your baby has fewer wet or dirty nappies than expected.
Your baby is not gaining weight.
urgent: No wet nappy at all, or your baby is very sleepy and will not wake for feeds.

jaundice.title: My newborn looks yellow
jaundice.intro: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes is called jaundice. It is common in newborns and usually harmless.
common: It is most noticeable around day 3 and usually fades within about 2 weeks.
It often starts on the face and can spread down the body.
On brown or black skin it is easier to see in the whites of the eyes, inside the mouth or on the palms.
It happens because a newborn's liver is still developing.
helps: Feed often, 8 to 12 times a day. Wake a sleepy baby for feeds.
Check your baby in daylight.
Tell your midwife or doctor if you notice yellowing. Most babies need no treatment.
Do not put your baby in the sun to treat jaundice. It does not work and can burn the skin.
help: You think your baby has jaundice.
The yellowing gets worse or lasts longer than 2 weeks. Breastfed babies can stay a little yellow for longer, but always check with your doctor.
Your baby's wee is dark yellow or brown. Keep a nappy to show.
urgent: Your baby's poo is pale or chalky. Keep a nappy to show.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours after birth.
Your baby is very sleepy, hard to wake or not feeding.
Your baby is floppy, stiff or has jerking movements.
A temperature of 38°C or higher, or 36°C or lower.
Trouble breathing, or no wet nappies.

baby_poo.title: Is my baby's poo normal?
baby_poo.intro: Baby poo changes a lot in the first week. Its colour and how often your baby poos vary, and most changes are normal.
common: The first poos are black-green and sticky. This is called meconium.
Over the first days they turn green-brown, then yellow by about day 5 to 7.
Breastfed babies' poo is often runny and yellow, with little seeds. Formula-fed babies' poo is usually firmer and browner.
Some breastfed babies go a few days without a poo, and that can be normal if feeding and weight gain are good.
helps: Keep track of nappies in the first weeks. It shows whether feeding is going well.
Take a photo of an unusual nappy to show your midwife or doctor.
Change nappies often and clean gently with water to protect the skin.
help: Your baby strains a lot, has hard poos or seems constipated.
Poo stays black after the first few days.
Diarrhoea lasts more than 1 or 2 days.
urgent: Poo is pale, white or chalky.
There is blood in their poo.
Your baby is very unwell, floppy or not feeding.

choking.title: What do I do if my child chokes?
choking.intro: It only takes a few minutes to learn what to do. A first aid course for parents is the best way to practise. It teaches the method used where you live, which can differ slightly between countries.
common: A child who coughs loudly can usually clear the blockage on their own. Encourage the cough and stay close.
A silent cough, no crying or not being able to breathe in is an emergency.
Gagging on new food is common and different from choking.
helps: If coughing does not clear the blockage, shout for help and ask someone to call your emergency number. Do not leave your child.
Baby under 1: lay the baby face down along your thigh, with their head supported and lower than their body. Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
If still blocked: turn the baby face up, head lower, and give up to 5 chest thrusts with 2 fingers in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line.
Child over 1: give up to 5 back blows with the child leaning forward. Then give up to 5 tummy thrusts: stand behind them, put your fist between their belly button and ribs, and pull in and up.
Check the mouth after each blow or thrust. Do not poke blindly with your fingers.
Repeat the cycle until the object comes out or help arrives.
help: You have given back blows or thrusts, even if the object came out.
urgent: The blockage does not clear after back blows and thrusts. Call your emergency number and keep going.
Your child stops responding. Call your emergency number on speaker and start rescue breathing and chest compressions if you know how.

home_safety.title: How do I make my home safe?
home_safety.intro: Babies move faster than you expect. A few simple changes prevent most common accidents at home.
common: Falls, choking, burns, poisoning and drowning are the most common accidents for children under 5.
Risks change as your child learns to roll, crawl, climb and open things.
helps: Change nappies on the floor if you can. Never leave your baby alone on a changing table, bed or sofa.
Fit safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs, and locks on windows.
Keep small objects, button batteries and magnets out of reach.
Lock away medicines, cleaning products and laundry capsules.
Keep hot drinks out of reach. Run cold water first when filling the bath and check the temperature.
Stay within arm's reach when your child is in the bath, and empty paddling pools after use.
Tie blind and curtain cords out of reach. Fit smoke alarms and test them every month.
help: You would like advice on home safety or a first aid course near you.
urgent: Your child has swallowed a button battery, a magnet, medicine or a cleaning product. Call your emergency number or poison centre now. Do not make your child vomit, and do not give food or drink.
A burn that is larger than your child's palm, or on the face, hands or genitals. Cool it under running water while you get help.

sun_safety.title: How do I protect my child in the sun?
sun_safety.intro: Young skin burns easily. Shade, clothing and sunscreen together keep children safe in the sun.
common: Babies under 6 months should be kept out of direct sun. Sunscreen is not recommended at this age.
The sun is strongest in the middle of the day, roughly 11:00 to 15:00.
Children get hot and thirsty faster than adults.
helps: Use shade, a parasol or a sunshade. Do not cover the pram with a blanket, which can cause overheating.
Dress your child in light, loose clothes, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses.
From 6 months, use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher that protects against UVA and UVB. Reapply every 2 hours and after time in water.
Offer extra feeds to babies, and water to older babies and children.
Never leave a child in a parked car.
help: Your child has sunburn with blisters, or seems unwell after time in the sun.
urgent: Signs of heatstroke: very hot skin, confusion, fast breathing, floppiness, or not responding normally.

toddler_sleep.title: My toddler will not go to bed
toddler_sleep.intro: Bedtime battles and night waking are common between 1 and 5 years. A calm routine and patience help most children.
common: Toddlers need about 11 to 14 hours of sleep a day, including naps. Children aged 3 to 5 need about 10 to 13 hours.
Getting up again, calling out and fear of the dark are common.
Big changes, such as a new sibling or starting daycare, can upset sleep for a while.
helps: Keep a calm routine at the same time every night: bath, pyjamas, teeth, one story, goodnight.
Start the routine about 30 minutes before your child usually falls asleep, then move bedtime earlier slowly.
Turn screens off 30 to 60 minutes before bed.
If your child gets up, take them back to bed calmly and briefly, every time.
A night light or a favourite toy can help with fears.
Avoid long naps late in the afternoon.
help: Sleep problems are affecting the whole family.
Your child snores loudly or seems to stop breathing for short periods while asleep.
You need support with a sleep plan.

daycare.title: Starting daycare
daycare.intro: Starting daycare is a big step for children and parents. Most children settle well with a slow start and a clear goodbye.
common: Crying at drop-off is common in the first weeks and often stops soon after you leave.
Children may be more tired, clingy or grumpy at home while they settle.
More colds are common in the first year of daycare.
helps: Start slowly: short visits together, then short periods alone, then full days.
Say a clear, short goodbye and tell your child when you will be back, for example after lunch. Then leave.
Do not sneak out. It can make children more worried next time.
Bring a comfort item from home.
Plan quiet time and an early bedtime on daycare days.
Talk with the carers and share your child's routines.
help: Your child is still very upset after several weeks.
Your child stops eating or sleeping well.
You are worried about how your child is cared for. Talk to the staff first.

biting.title: My toddler bites or hits
biting.intro: Biting, hitting, pinching and hair-pulling are common in babies and toddlers. This is part of normal development and usually passes.
common: Toddlers often bite or hit when excited, angry or frustrated, before they have the words for their feelings.
Tiredness, hunger and noisy, busy places make it more likely.
Teething can lead babies to bite.
helps: Stay calm. Say a firm "No, biting hurts" and move your child away.
First, give attention to the child who was hurt.
Name the feeling: "You are angry because he took the car."
Later, when everyone is calm, show your child what to do instead: say "Stop", ask for help or stamp their feet.
Praise gentle touches and kind play.
Never bite or hit back. It teaches that hurting is fine.
help: It happens very often or is getting worse despite your efforts.
You feel angry, exhausted or unable to cope.
Daycare staff are worried about it.

parent_tired.title: I am exhausted all the time
parent_tired.intro: Feeling tired almost all the time is very common when you look after a baby or young child. Broken sleep adds up, and it is not a sign that you are doing anything wrong.
common: Babies wake at night to feed for many months. Many toddlers still wake some nights too.
Lack of sleep can make you forgetful, irritable, tearful and slow to react.
If you gave birth, your body also needs time to recover. Feeding a baby uses a lot of energy too.
Tiredness usually gets easier as your child starts to sleep for longer stretches.
helps: Sleep or rest when your baby sleeps, even for 20 minutes. Let some chores wait.
Share night wakings if you can. Take turns, or let someone do an early morning so you can sleep on.
Accept offers of help with meals, shopping, washing or a short walk with the baby.
Eat regular meals and snacks, drink water and get outside in daylight for a short time each day.
Go to bed early on some nights. Keep caffeine for the morning and put your phone away an hour before bed.
If you feel you might fall asleep while feeding, put your baby down in their own cot first. Never fall asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair.
help: You have felt tired for a few weeks and rest does not help.
Tiredness makes daily life hard, or you also feel low or anxious most of the time. See the guide on low mood.

You also feel breathless, dizzy, notice a racing heartbeat, look pale, or have lost or gained weight without trying. Your doctor can check your blood for anaemia and thyroid problems, which can happen after birth.
You cannot sleep even when you have the chance.
urgent: You are so tired that you feel unable to care for your baby safely. Put your baby down safely in their cot and call someone to come and help now.
You have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Get help now: call your emergency number or a crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency department.

parent_anxiety.title: I worry all the time
parent_anxiety.intro: Some worry is normal when you are expecting or caring for a baby. But if worry fills most of your day or stops you resting, it may be anxiety, which is common and treatable.
common: About 1 in 8 women have anxiety during pregnancy. It is also common in the first year after birth, and partners can be affected too.
Anxiety can feel like racing thoughts, always expecting the worst, feeling on edge, a tight chest, a churning stomach or poor sleep.
A panic attack is a sudden rush of fear with a racing heart, shaking, sweating or breathlessness. Most last between 5 and 20 minutes. They feel frightening but are not dangerous.

Many new parents have sudden, unwanted thoughts or images of their baby being hurt. Sometimes the thought is of hurting the baby themselves. These thoughts are very common. Having a thought does not mean you will act on it.
helps: Tell someone you trust how you feel. Saying it out loud often makes the worry smaller.
During a panic attack, stay where you are and breathe slowly in and out. Remind yourself that it will pass.
Try not to fight or push away unwanted thoughts. Notice them, let them pass and turn back to what you were doing.
Limit time spent searching online for worries. Write down your questions and ask your doctor, midwife or health visitor.
Move your body each day, even a 10 minute walk, and rest when you can.
Cut down on caffeine and avoid using alcohol to cope.
help: Worry is strong, lasts more than 2 weeks, or makes daily life hard.
You have panic attacks, or you avoid things because you fear one.
Unwanted thoughts come many times a day, upset you a lot, or make you avoid caring for your baby. Talking therapy works well for this.
You also feel low most of the time. See the guide on low mood.
urgent: You have thoughts of harming yourself, or you feel you might act on thoughts of harming your baby. Get help now: call your emergency number or a crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency department.

You or someone close to you notices sudden changes after birth: confusion, seeing or hearing things that are not there, very strange beliefs, or a very high or fast-changing mood. This most often starts in the first 2 weeks. It is a medical emergency. Get help now: call your emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department.
You have chest pain or sudden breathlessness that is new to you, especially in pregnancy or after birth. Do not assume it is panic. Call your emergency number.

parent_body.title: My body feels different after birth
parent_body.intro: Your body has done a huge job, and it takes time to recover. Many changes in the first weeks are normal, and most get better with time and gentle care.
common: Bleeding from the vagina (lochia) is heavy at first, then turns brown and lighter. It usually stops by 6 to 8 weeks, but can last longer.
Period-like cramps are common in the first days, especially during breastfeeding.
Leaking a little urine when you cough, laugh or move suddenly is common after birth.

After a caesarean, pain can last several weeks. Avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby at first. Do not drive until you can wear a seatbelt and brake hard without pain. This often takes about 6 weeks.
Many health services offer a postnatal check around 6 to 8 weeks after birth. It is a time to talk about your recovery, your mood, contraception and anything that worries you.
helps: Use pads, not tampons, while you are bleeding. Wash stitches or your wound gently each day with plain warm water and pat dry.
Start pelvic floor exercises when you feel ready. Squeeze and lift the muscles you use to stop a wee, hold for a few seconds, then relax. Repeat a few times each day.
Walk a little every day. Wait until after your postnatal check before high-impact exercise such as running.
Have sex only when you feel ready. There is no set time. If it hurts, stop and tell your doctor.
You can get pregnant from 3 weeks after birth, even if you are breastfeeding and your periods have not come back. Use contraception if you do not want another pregnancy.
Rest, eat well and drink plenty of water, especially if you are breastfeeding.
help: Bleeding gets heavier, smells unusual, or has not eased after 6 to 8 weeks.
Your stitches or caesarean wound become more red, swollen or painful, or leak pus.
You still leak urine or wind, or have pain during sex, after your postnatal check.
You feel pain or burning when you pass urine, or you are worried about any part of your recovery.
urgent: Very heavy bleeding, large clots, or bleeding with feeling faint, dizzy or a pounding heart. Call your emergency number.
A high temperature with tummy pain, foul-smelling discharge or feeling very unwell. These can be signs of a serious infection. Get help now: call your emergency number.

Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, pain or swelling in the calf of 1 leg, or a severe headache with changes in your vision or vomiting. Get help now: call your emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department.

parent_couple.title: Our relationship has changed since the baby
parent_couple.intro: Having a baby puts a strain on most relationships, however strong they were before. Less sleep and less time together are hard for everyone, and the most demanding stage does not last forever.
common: Many couples argue more in the first year, often about sleep, chores and money.
1 partner may feel left out, or feel that they do more than their share.
Interest in sex often drops for a while because of tiredness, healing and hormones.
Single parents and parents who share care from 2 homes feel this pressure too, often with less time to rest.
helps: Agree together who does which night wakings and which chores. Write it down and check it again after a few weeks.
Say clearly what you need. Your partner cannot guess. Try "I need 1 hour to sleep" instead of "You never help".
Find 10 minutes a day to talk about something other than the baby.
Stay close in small ways, such as a hug, holding hands or a short walk together. Closeness does not have to mean sex.
If you parent apart, keep messages about your child short, calm and practical.
Ask family and friends for the help you actually need, and keep in touch with people who support you.
help: You argue most days, or arguments do not get resolved.
You feel afraid of your partner, or conflict starts to feel unsafe.
You or your partner feel low or anxious most of the time. See the guide on low mood.
Your doctor, midwife or health visitor can listen and tell you about counselling and other support near you.
urgent: You or your children are in danger right now. Call your emergency number.

Someone hurts you, threatens you, controls your money or who you see, or forces you into sex. This is domestic abuse. It often starts or gets worse in pregnancy or after birth. You do not have to wait for an emergency to get help. Tell your doctor, midwife or health visitor.

parent_work.title: I am going back to work
parent_work.intro: Going back to work after time with your child brings many feelings at once. Guilt, worry, relief and excitement are all normal, often on the same day.
common: Many children take a few weeks to settle in a new childcare setting. Tears at drop-off are common and often stop soon after you leave.
Children in childcare often catch many colds and stomach bugs in the first year.
The first weeks back can feel very tiring as everyone gets used to new routines.
You can keep breastfeeding when you go back to work if you wish. Many parents feed before and after work and express milk during the day.
helps: Ask your childcare how they settle new children. Most start with short visits that get longer over time. Try to begin this before your first day back.
Say a short, warm goodbye and leave. Ask the carer to send you a message once your child has settled.
If you want to keep breastfeeding, tell your employer before you return and ask for a private place and time to express. Practise expressing a few weeks before.
Store expressed milk at the back of the fridge. Use it within 3 days, or freeze it if you will not use it by then. Label each portion with the date.
Make a plan for days when your child is sick and cannot go to childcare. Think about who could help, such as a partner, family or friends.
Keep some time for yourself each week, even 30 minutes, and keep your evenings simple at first.
help: You feel low, anxious or unable to cope for more than 2 weeks. See the guide on low mood.
Worry about your child or your work stops you sleeping or enjoying anything.
You are worried about how your child is settling after several weeks.
urgent: You have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Get help now: call your emergency number or a crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency department.

charger.name: Phone charger with a long cable

nightwear.name: Nightwear that opens at the front, if you plan to breastfeed

bras.name: 2 or 3 comfortable bras and breast pads
